speechtext: I wish to bring the attention of the government to matters regarding the maple sugar industry which are d'actualite in our province.

maintopic: HON. D. D. MACKENZIE APPOINTMENT TO THE BENCH
speechtext: Very well.

maintopic: HON. D. D. MACKENZIE APPOINTMENT TO THE BENCH
speechtext: The first is that in view' of the low price of the article and the high price of firewood, maple trees are being cut down when they really should remain to be tapped. The association does not ask for the expenditure of money, on which fact they are to be congratulated, but merely that an educational campaign should be inaugurated, no doubt by the Department of Agriculture, to show the unwisdom of such proceeding. speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would ask the attention of the committee to item 435, being a supplementary estimate to provide for the bonus to civil servants. Has the government given any consideration to the question of making permanent the bonus that is at present paid to civil servants of the lower classes? I have had a great many requests from members of the outside service particularly asking me to support a resolution of that character. I have not so far arrived at any conclusion on the subject and I think there should be a declaration of policy from the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government has not felt that the present is an opportune time to consider any final revision of salaries, largely for the reason that this year there have been exceptional conditions affecting the cost of living, such for example as the high price of coal which obtained last year. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the policy.
This is the same bonus as given last year and two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not quite the same as that which was given two years ago. The bonus paid last year was similiar to that of the previous year, with certain exceptions which were mentioned at the time; but this year it is the same as last year's.
It is as much as it was two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is what
we are trying to do.

I hope the government
is satisfied with its progress-

speechtext: Oh yes.

-in reducing the cost
of living.

speechtext:
It is coming
down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Every day in every
way-
You are getting worse.

Is it a fact that civil
servants with dependents receive a larger salary than those without dependents?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend says "salary;" no doubt he means the bonus which we are now discussing. If he is referring to the bonus, it is true that civil servants having dependents are entitled to a larger bonus than those without dependents.

This applies, I take it, only to civil servants whose dependents are in Canada. I understand that those civil servants who have dependents overseas in Great Britain do not come within this class. I want to make this point, that while this is an excellent provision in behalf of civil servants, there are certain cases in which it is a distinct hardship to withhold the bonus from employees whose dependents happen to be overseas. I



Supply-Civil Service Bonus
know some civil servants whose mothers are too ill to leave the Old Country and the bonus is on that account withheld.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The whole
bonus scheme has been worked out by the Civil Service Commission, and no doubt if the point which my hon. friend has raised were brought to its attention it would receive consideration by the commission.

The government cost
of living statistics show that since March, 1922, the cost of living has steadily risen. But not only do the government statistics and the curve of the Labour department, which I shall have in a moment, reveal this fact, but the statistics of Dun, of Professor Michell of McMaster University, and indeed all other Canadian statistics, show exactly the same thing. The curve of the cost of living is now about one point and thre'e quarters higher than it was when the government brought down its budget a year ago. The descent of the cost of living which commenced in July, 1920, and which was precipitate all through 1921, was arrested the very day this government assumed power. However, it resumed very slowly for about two months; but when the budget was brought down and went into effect it commenced to rise. It has risen ever since and is rising now; and it has risen most substantially in the last year. May I ask the government what change of policy they purpose adopting to reverse the effect of the policy they now actually have in operation?

I might ask my hon. friend a question, seeing that he has the information before him. Is it not true that different economists who have advanced the view that the cost of living is going up say that the largest percentage of the increase is attributable in the first place to rent, and in the second place to coal?

Well, I was not discussing the causes; and as a matter of fact these are not the causes, these -are elements. Rents are going up, coal is going up and wholesale commodities are also going up. I know that coal and rent are going up and in this country are very likely to continue to do so. But the government abandoned the unemployed last winter with the result that they drifted across to the United States, and now there is no one to build. We cannot improve our housing facilities without mechanics, and we are without them; they are now citizens of the United States.

Those who want to build can build. They have the mechanics and the
[Mr. Irvine.[
labourers down my way and they are building there.
I am sorry to say my hon. friend is wrong. There are portions of Canada that are virtually without mechanics altogether.
Portions?
Yes. There are portions that are wholly stripped of mechanics.
Where the calamity howlers live.

So from what we have heard from the Minister of Trade and Commerce there does not appear to be very much hope for the immediate future. He will remember how his Minister of Labour complained in 1921 of the noble struggle that he had made to get the cost of living down and to take from >
profiteers that fraction that should be added to the earnings of the workingman. He was wholly unsuccessful, as he stated, notwithstanding that fact that all through that period, from the middle of 1920 right to the end of 1921, there was a very rapid descent of the cost of living curve. He was not satisfied and complained that he was only allowed a wooden gun with which to go out after profiteers and get the cost of living down. Perhaps his colleagues or the Prime Minister will explain what kind of a gun he has had since. He has been much less successful. In fact, the operation that was well under way was arrested immediately he got into office and the reverse process has been in operation ever since and looks as if it would continue for some time. The cost of living in Canada, even at its worst, was lower according to official figures than the cost of living even in the United States and much lower than in other countries. That was the case right up to the time of the coming into power of this government. I do not think that can be said to be the case to-day. I think it will be found that the cost of living in the United States, making allowance for the difference in the method of calculation, is to-day lower than here, and our prospects for the immediate future, considering the process that has gone on in the way of the depletion of our workingmen, are not good. I should like to have the government's view of this question, as to what kind of gun they purpose giving the Minister of Labour from this on that will be an improvement upon the weapon that he has had; and as to when they expect to succeed in the noble struggle they are making against the cost of

Supply-Civil Service Bonus
living, so that we will not be faced with this vote continuously for years to come.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As respects the operation of economic laws, I think my right hon. friend will recognize that cause and effect do not operate simultaneously, but that usually the effect of the operation of certain causes is only experienced at some later period. He says that the moment this government took office the cost of living began to rise. If that was the case it must have been due to causes that were set in motion while my right hon. friend was in office.

I did not say that. I said that the descent that took place while we were in office was arrested. It proceeded to go down a little for about three months until the government's budget went into operation, after which it immediately proceeded to rise. It is quite true it was a case of cause and effect: the government's budget was the immediate cause, and the high cost of living is the effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The only defect in my right hon. friend's reasoning is that his operation of cause and effect is a little more instantaneous than that which is commonly observed in regard to economic forces. Any study of economic questions will reveal that these matters are not worked out in a week, a month or even a series of months; indeed sometimes they cover several years.
What was the cause of the great descent through 1921?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Occasionally
special causes operate and help to explain special conditions. The increased cost of living this past winter would almost seem to be elementary in its explanation to anyone who appreciates the important part that coal plays in the cost of production and the genera! cost of living. As my right hon. friend knows, Canada has need of coal earlier in the season than the United States, our need of coal extends over a longer period, and the increase in its cost increases the cost of transportation, the cost of manufacture, the cost of running retail establishments, the cost of management of households-it enters into every particular that one can have regard to dealing with the economic situation. Under those circumstances it was inevitable that the cost of living curve should be higher this year than possiblv in previous years. There may be other explanations, but I think this is an all-sufficient one to account for any exceptional rise this year.
115J

How does the Prime Minister figure out, that there has been an increased cost in the price of coal? Speaking1 for the Maritime provinces, where we use very largely soft coal, I can assure him that coal has been much cheaper during the entire year than it was a year ago. That coal goes as far west as Montreal and supplies the manufacturing establishments of the pro-' vince of Quebec and of the Maritime' provinces. I cannot speak for the province" of Ontario, but I would advise the right hon. gentleman that there was no scarcity of coal for manufacturing purposes in the eastern provinces, and that there was not only no increase in the cost, but an actual decrease both in the cost of production and the freight rates, due to a special rate having been put into .effect as far west as Montreal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend has referred to "cost" all the way through.
I do not know whether he intends to refer to. price, but if he means the price of coal I do not think he need go beyond this chamber to have every hon. member present witness to the circumstance that the increase in the price of coal has been very considerable all through this past winter.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a suggestion to the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). I think we have a very good gun in this part of the House for reducing the cost of living, and I hope the right hon. gentleman, probably next week, will help us supply some of the amt-munition.

If I help the hon. gentleman to supply it I am afraid the reverse effect would take place. I was warned only last night that my support always turned the government the other way. I shall watch with great interest the operation of the hon. gentleman's efforts oh the budget this session, but I would remind him that the big factor in the increased cost of living is the SO per cent increase in the sales tax. That is the main legislative cause of the higher cost of living. The Prime Minister is now very deferential to the effect of economic law* and world forces and cause and effect. I cannot recall those words falling from his lips in the discussion of 1921. Then those things were wholly absent. It was altogether a case of enabling the present Minister of Labour to have a gun to go after profiteers. But what I want to emphasize is that not only in respect to rent and coal which he mentions now-the latter of which only in a certain portion of Canada and as to one
Supply-Civil Service Bonus

class has risen in value at all-but as respects food stuffs, clothing and the essential factors and necessaries of life the cost of living has continuously risen since the hon. gentlemen took the treasury benches and put their taxation measures into effect. That has been the result ever since, and as a consequence we are called upon to vote five and a half million dollars to-day, and next year we will be called upon to vote the same amount according to present tendencies. Now, will the Prime Minister or any member of his government state when they hope by the success of their anticost of living operations to get rid of this vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend says that the vote is increased so much this year over the period during which he held office.

No, I did not say that. I [DOT]said that we are called upon to vote this much this year for the cost of living bonus. This is virtually the same as we had in 1921, and it is the same as we had last year. In 1921 the cost of living was rapidly going down; now it is rising. I know that prior to that time the cost of living was higher than it is now, but I also know that relatively to other countries of the world it was lower in Canada that it is to-day. That is how the government is to be tested-by its own policy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before I
answer my right hon .friend, will he admit that the sum we are asking to-day for bonus is virtually the same as it was in 1921?
I will admit that the Prime Minister said so himself. I asked him at the opening of this discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, I have the figures before me now, and I can give my right hon. friend the exact information. In 1920-21 my right hon. friend asked the House, for the purposes of the cost of living bonus, for an appropriation of $12,500,000.
That was three years ago

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am keeping to the 1921 period, which was the one my right hon. friend referred to, and is the period during which his government was in office. He asked parliament then for an appropriation of $12,500,000, of which his government spent in bonus $10,588,890.
With the cost of living going down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In 1921-22-that includes the other part of 1921-he asked parliament for an appropriation of $9,375,000, of which his government spent in bonus $7,710,264. When this government came into office we asked for an appropriation for bonus of $5,500,000 as against the $9,375,000 that my right hon. friend had asked for one year and the $12,500,000 he had asked for the year before. This year we are asking for the same amount as last year, namely, $5,500,000.

The amount spent two years ago was about the same. The amount asked for now is some five millions and a half. The Prime Minister stated at the opening of the discussion that this was the same cost ol * living bonus as that of a year ago and as that of two years ago, save in respect to certain adjustments that had been made of a detailed character. He will find, if he goes into it, that it is the same; naturally as we recede from the war it does not apply on as large a volume. It did not apply last year on as large as the year before because of the reduction in staff that we had made in 1921. But the cost of living bonus to-day to the individual is virtually the same as it was two years ago, and if this process continues the government is going to have to increase it.
Mr. SHAWT; In view of the admitted increase in the cost of living over that of last year, has the government considered the advisability of increasing this vote for the present year? In any event, upon what reasoning has the decision been arrived at that the bonus should not be increased over that of last year?
Mr. MACKENZIE KING; The bonus was never intended to correspond automatically with the increase or decrease in the cost of living. It is a general allowance intended to meet exceptional circumstances. The government thinks that having regard to the possible further reduction in the cost of living before the year is much further advanced, this amount will be quite sufficient for the purpose.

Civil government-Post Office-salaries and contingencies, $1,271,448.

I move that item 19 be amended by inserting after the word "salaries" the words, "including Superintendent of Mail Contracts at $5,400 per annum." These words appeared in the estimates as prepared but

Supply-Post Office
were inadvertently omitted from the printed estimates. The amount of the vote is not affected, as the increase made is already provided for in the item.
I would like to ask the minister how much he is being helped to-day in one of his three activities-his postal activities-by his genial friend the Minister of Customs and Excise.
To the extent of moving the resolution.
Now we have got step number one. I want to know how much money is being credited to the Post Office Department which is taken in by way of taxation not connected with the postal service?

We have carried on the same system that was put in force by my hon. friend when he was administering the War Measures Act. I have no hesitation in saying that it would be a good thing to provide that excise stamps should be used to pay excise taxes and postage stamps to pay postal charges. My hon. friend knows that it is very difficult to estimate how much money is- I will not say wrongly, but not exactly rightly collected-by my hon. friend the Postmaster General that ought to be credited to Customs and Excise.

What my hon. friend says is quite true as to the commencement of things. But where we then used one stamp for purposes not connected with the Post Office, to-day anywhere from five to twenty are used. Besides that, there are the stamps used on receipts, which have nothing to do with the postal service; so that the use of stamps for these purposes has been enormously multiplied. Surely the department has some idea how much of the revenues are properly attributable to their own activities and how much to the postal service.

It is impossible to make any definite accounting in this respect. Either postal or excise stamps may be used for All these purposes which are not connected with postal charges, and unless you make an audit of everybody's books, the accounts of the banks, and so on, you cannot tell how many postage stamps have been used on cheques, receipts, etc. Under the present system that cannot be done. You might arrive at a kind of average. I take it that there is no increase in the volume of business done by the Post Office Department to account for any substantial increase in revenue.	_ j
There has been really none, as I understand it. The volume of mail carried is practically the same as a year or two years ago; indeed, less than three years ago undoubtedly.

To do that we would have to ascertain the revenue of the Post Office three years ago and say that the balance comes from excise, but that would not be an accurate estimate. We cannot do that as the law stands to-day. I would ask nothing better than to change the law so that every excise duty would be payable with an excise stamp. Then we could know the revenue we were getting out of stamps, but as it is now, we cannot. Would the people stand for such a change in the law? Would they say it was too much inconvenience to carry excise stamps in their pockets as well as postage stamps? I do not know. I would be willing to take a chance on that, in order that the revenue could be credited where it belongs, and that could be done if we had postage stamps for postal business and excise stamps for excise duties.
My latter question, in fact, all the questions were addressed to the Acting Postmaster General.
You wanted to know how far the excise tax was responsible, and I wanted to help by stating the case.
I am quite willing to admit that my hon. friend is of great assistance in any cause in which he is en- ' gaged.
Do not get sarcastic. It is your law that is there when it comes to customs; the mistake is yours.

I still say that I was talking to the Acting Postmaster General. Now we can arrive approximately at what we are after. For example, what was the amount of mail matter carried during each of the three last years? Knowing that, and knowing that there is no change whatever in the rates for carrying it, we can get a pretty good approximate idea of how much excise has helped out the Post Office Department.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Acting Postmaster General): It is very difficult to get at an accurate statement for the reasons mentioned by the Minister of Customs. I have some sympathy, as a private individual, with the suggestion of the Minister of Customs that these two things should be kept separate and that the Customs and Excise department should get credit for receipts from the stamp tax for which it is responsible; but
Supply-Post Office

as Acting Postmaster General I take umbrage against it. As a matter of fact, I think the amount received from the war tax last year appears in the Postmaster General's report, it is about $7,400,000, if I remember correctly.
My hon. friend knows that is not covering the question at all.

I thought that was exactly what my hon. friend asked me

how much was received by the Post Office Department on account of sale of stamps used under the war tax.

My hon. friend has not quite got the point. He has a war tax of his own, and he shows the war tax of his department in his report. Am I wrong in that? What I was asking was the amount of stamp revenue which you got under these other war measures of taxation. I think the minister will find I am right.

I took the figures in the Postmaster General's report, where the revenue from the war tax is given as about $7,400,000. It does not say that it represents the one cent extra of postage. I think it is an estimate of the amount from the entire sale of stamps on account of war tax. Whether that includes the stamp tax as we have it in the other form, I do not know. If it does not, I can see no way of getting the information, unless we give an approximate estimate.
Might I suggest that the acting minister ask his representative here, who I suppose knows something about the department, as to how that amount is made up?
I am informed that this item in the Postmaster General's report refers to the proportional increase in the postal revenue from the increased letter postage.

Then I understand that we are at one on that. The minister now knows that this extra amount raised and shown in the report has nothing whatever to do with stamps on cheques and stamps on receipts, but is merely the extra cent put on postage. We are on common ground there.
Mr.' GRAHAM: That is approximately it, I suppose.
I do not know whether it is approximately it or not. Surely you know. I ask who this gentleman is that is advising the minister.
He is one of the officials of the Post Office Department, and a very efficient man.
Which official? I want to know if he is the gentleman who is running the department now.
He is chief clerk in the Secretary's branch in charge of estimates.
Might I ask whether the gentleman is running the department now?
He is in charge of the estimates, and very properly so.
I am not saying anything against the gentleman. I am sure he is absolutely all right. I just want to know for information. If he is not running the department, who is?
So far as responsibility to the country is concerned, the Acting Postmaster General.
Hear, hear. Good doctrine.
Now so far as the work goes, who is running the department?
Each branch is carrying on its work as usual, reporting to the acting minister instead of to the minister, who is absent through illness.
I thought they usually report to the deputy, and the deputy to the minister. Who are the sub-heads reporting to now?
Mr. Murphy, no relation of the minister, is acting deputy minister, and Mr. Coolican is general superintendent of the postal service.
Now will the minister kindly tell me what the amount of mail carried was, the weight of the mail last year?

I have not the particulars of that here. The mails are not weighed altogether. Under the new arrangement a great deal of mail is carried by the square foot; it is carried on the space basis, and not weighed.

I am perfectly willing to help the minister in every possible way. If he wants to give the information by the square foot let us have it by the square foot. If he cannot give it by pounds, let us have it by the square foot, or any way he likes to give it.
By the gallon.
By the gallon perhaps.

That is my measure.

That would be the most popular measure, I presume. As a matter of fact, I have not that information here. I could put the accountants to work and get it in -a few days, but that information has never been asked for in the House before in connection with the estimates. It is the expenditure, rather than the square foot or the number of pounds, that the country is interested in.

I have always thought that there was a record kept of the volume of business done, and I think my hon. friend will find that such a record is kept in the department. I have even seen the totals of the letters handled in different offices given at different times.
That is the amount, not the tons.
Then we will take the amount. If my hon. friend does not want to give me the information by weight, or by the square foot, will he give me the number of letters handled last year?

We have not the information, though as I said before, we might get it by putting accountants to work and going through various returns, but that kind of information was never before contemplated as likely to be asked for in this House; it never was dreamed of. I know what my hon. friend is trying to get at. He is trying to find out, if I understand him, what the return Would be from stamps used otherwise than on letters.

Certainly. In
other words we want to know your postal business and we cannot get the information.

I have been asking that
question for some days in connection with the Customs department, because my hon. friend and myself have several times discussed the point as to what the proportion of money received from the stamp tax was. Now the Post Office Department sells these postage stamps but there is no way of discovering where or how the revenue should go. A stamp vendor anywhere in the country sells his stamps to John Smith, and John Smith may put those stamps on cheques or he may put them on letters. Of course an estimate might be made. If we had the receipts from the stamps which are placed on cheques we could find out then how much money is received from that source. There is this other fact: the stamp vendors get a percentage of their sales.

The matter then amounts to this-that the minister is not in a position
to say to-day whether there is a- deficit or whether there is a surplus in the operation of the Post Office Department. I mention this because the Postmaster General himself, has, on various occasions, inspired the publication of items in newspapers supporting the administration to the effect that owing to the great economies which he has effected in the department he has realized a fine surplus. Now we know that the claim is false, the assumption is untrue, it cannot possibly be justified for the reasons which the Acting Postmaster General has given.

It is a fact that the business done in 1922, by all the tests that could be applied would certainly be not more and would probably be somewhat less than in 1921. All the other tax returns of the government would go to establish it. Now, assuming that, we must at least infer that the increased revenue this year over last year is due to the increased stamp tax for the nine months. That increased revenue, as I recall, is between three and four million dollars-about $3,000,000. That would be equivalent to something over 14,000,000 for the entire year. So that the government, by these extra taxes, is taking that amount
4 p.m. of money yearly from the pockets of the people. This has caused the Postmaster General periodically to make newspaper exclamations regarding the magnificent management of the Post Office Department, and afforded stump speakers, including hon. members opposite, in by-elections the only thing that had even the outward appearance of an argument in favour of the contention that they were able to present. I heard many and many a time about the magnificent management of the Post Office Department, in that we had a surplus this year. I really felt some. compassion for the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) when his colleague was taking the credit for taxes that he had assumed the onus of putting on. It did not seem quite fair to me that the Postmaster General should be boasting before the whole Dominion that he had been able to produce a surplus in that department because of the mere fact that the Excise department was taxing the people at the rate of $4,000,000 a year extra for stamps. It costs nothing to sell these stamps, or virtually nothing. Notwithstanding that though, the cost of management of the Post Office Department is annually increasing. The estimates this year show an amount very substantially more than last year. I would not think it should be more at all, because these stamps cost nothing to sell; what costs
Royal Assent

in the Post Office Department is the handling of mail and mail matter. The fact, then, appears to be that instead of having more economical management we have had less; and instead of having a modest, truthful presentation of the facts we have had periodical boasting which really is nothing more than claiming credit for taxing the people.
It is a mistake to think that it does not cost anything to sell stamps, but that is immaterial. It sometimes costs 50 per cent, and in other instances 20 per cent.

That commission goes
against the salaries.
The fact is it costs money to sell these stamps.
Take it all through, it does not require 10 per cent to sell the stamps or near that.

I have not figured out the average. In a good many cases it costs 20 per cent, in others 40 per cent, and in others again 50 per cent; I do not think there is any question about it. I am not trying to pretend that the Post Office revenue has not been swollen by the stamp tax, I admit it has, but to what extent I have been unable to find out. I have tried in various ways to ascertain, but there does not seem to be any system of accounting to cover that point- that is any system which makes a distinction between the two classes of stamps. The revenue of the Post Office Department must, of necessity, be swollen considerably by the sale of stamps that are not used for postage.
Where is the printing done?
The stamps are printed by the American Bank Note Company under contract with the Finance department.
But the other printing business, where is that done?
At the Printing bureau.
Is it all done there?
I imagine it is practically all done there.
I am given to understand that there is some printing done outside the Printing bureau. Can the minister inform me as to that?

subtopic: SITTING SUSPENDED FOR ROYAL ASSENT TO BILLS

speechtext:
A message was delivered by Colonel Ernest J. Chambers, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:

Mr. Speaker, His Honour the Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the Chamber of the Honourable the Senate.
Accordingly the House went up to the Senate,	[DOT]
And having returned,
Mr. Speaker informed the House that the Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General had been pleased to give in His Majesty's name the Royal Assent to the following bills:
An Act to provide for further advances to the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners.

An Act for the relief of Blanche Hilton.
An	Act	for	the	relief	of	May Woodbridge.An	Act	for	the	relief	of	Alice May Smith.An	Act	for	the	relief	of	Albert Ernest Mould.An	Act	for	the	relief	of	Winifred Rose Foster.
An Act for the relief of Emily May Small.

An	Act	for	the	relief	of	Ernest Warren Porter.An	Act	for	the	relief	of	May Elizabeth Meng.
