The House resumed in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Civil government-Post Office-salaries and contingencies, $1,271,448.

I think I am in a position now to give fairly accurately the information sought for in reference to the probable amount of revenue derived from the stamp tax this year in excess of that of last year. Last year the whole issue of stamps was approximately
828,000,000. This year it is estimated that at the end of the year it will be about $29,750,000. That is the issue. The officials have estimated that the sale this year will exceed the sale of last year by about $1,250,000.

I would ask the minister, if I might, why he does not compel the public to put revenue stamps on their cheques? Last year the government imposed a very heavy tax in the way of stamps to be placed on cheques, and this was done by means of putting

Supply-Post Office
on ordinary postage stamps. Had the government compelled the public at very small inconvenience-or, as I hold, at practically no inconvenience-to buy revenue stamps, the confusion which we have been talking about all afternoon would have been avoided, because each branch would then have its revenue properly credited to it, and the work would be done a great deal cheaper. When you buy stamps to put on your cheque in a country town the post office official gets from 30 to 40 per cent of their face value. This is his commission; in other words, we are imposing a tax upon the public and are paying 30 to 40 per cent for the cost of collecting this particular tax. Take any other tax, such as the income tax, and you will find that the government will claim that the collection can be made for from 3 to 4 per cent. Why is not this system adopted in connection with this particular tax for the collection of which we are paying between 30 and 40 per cent? The public could easily use revenue stamps and this would entail no inconvenience and no confusion. It may be claimed that it would be inconvenient and confusing, but this is not so, because when a man buys one class of stamps at the post office he can equally as well buy the other class. Moreover we have precedent to back us up. When the late government first introduced the tax, which was then a small one, it was provided that revenue or postage stamps might be affixed to cheques. But unfortunately the matter was left optional, and when anyone went to the post office he had the privilege of using either an excise stamp or the ordinary stamp. The postmaster of course, got 40 per cent on the postage stamps while he got only one per cent on the sale of the revenue or excise stamps, and like most people he pushed the sale of the article on which he, was getting the bigger profit. You might say you wanted revenue stamps and he would reply that postage stamps would do just as well and would add that he was short of revenue stamps. In the course of a few months therefore there was practically no sale for the revenue stamps. The mistake the government made at that time was in not making it compulsory for the public to use revenue stamps. The postmaster gets only one per cent on the sale of the revenue stamps, which can also be purchased from the banks, who get the same commission. If the government adopted exclusively the system of compelling the public to buy revenue stamps to put on cheques the inconvenience would be very slight and the profit to the country would be considerable. Besides this, all the confusion and dispute as to where the money should be
allocated would be obviated. I would ask the minister if there is any reason that he knows of in connection with the carrying out of this business why that system should not be adopted.

The only reason I have heard advanced against the system is the one of inconvenience to the public. There is a great difference of opinion upon that point. The average person buys postage stamps, and when people wish to issue cheques, in many cases the only place where they can get stamps keeps only the one kind. When the postage stamp is used for both purposes there is no confusion. It has been suggested to me that, under the conditions detailed by my hon. friend, the ordinary individual who used very few revenue stamps and a great many postage stamps might find himself putting revenue stamps on letters in spite of all his care, and putting postage stamps on cheques. Whether that reason is real or imaginary I am not prepared to say, but it is advanced at any rate. I might add that the public do not like taxes anyway, and if you impose them in the most inconvenient form they are annoying to say the least. There is a great deal to be said, however, in favour of having separate stamps for the two purposes. It would enable the Finance department or the Excise department to know exactly how effective any particular tax was. Take, for instance, the receipt tux. Under present conditions it is impossible accurately to state the revenue from the tax receipts. It can, of course, be estimated, but at best it is only an estimate, because the postage stamps that pass through the Postal, department are used on these receipts. If, there were a revenue stamp in use there would be no question at all, and the accounts between the Postal department and the Inland Revenue department would be cleanout, and we should have no discussion such as has taken place this afternoon in regard to the proper allocation of revenue. There is a good deal to be said on both sides. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) has had the matter under advisement for a considerable time, and had the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) been in good health and in the city they would probably have had some conferences concerning it. In the meantime I think I might say that on his return the matter will be discussed with the Minister of Customs because, as I have observed, there is much to be said on either side of the question. Certainly, from the standpoint of the accountants of the Finance department, it would be a great advantage to know what taxes were equitable

Supply-Post Office
and were really producing income, and this result would no doubt be effected by the use of separate stamps.

I would point out that it is no more embarrassing for a man to buy at the post office one dollar's worth of postage stamps and one dollar's worth of revenue stamps than it is for him to ask for a dollar's worth of 3-cent stamps and a dollar's worth of 2-cent stamps. He can do the one as easily as the other. I would point out also that although the method I have suggested might be slightly inconvenient, which I do not think it would be, the general public are getting educated, and if they knew, as they do know and as they realize, that the present method of collecting the tax is costing them 40 per cent whereas it would cost them only one per cent under the other system, they would undoubtedly put up with the trivial inconvenience that might be involved.

Why does it cost only 1 per cent to sell revenue stamps and as high as 40 per cent to sell postage stamps? I would hesitate a good while before I would change the present system, because I think there is a good deal in what the Acting Postmaster General says about the inconveniences such a change would be to the public. The amount of money that is gathered for revenue through the use of postage stamps on cheques is, I believe, somewhat exaggerated, for all the large business organizations use revenue stamps, and it is only in the smaller businesses and among private individuals that postage stamps are used for revenue purposes. I can quite understand the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) objecting to the present method-I * do not know whether he does or not, as a matter of fact-but it would be quite natural for him to do so, because apparently the Postmaster General now gets credit for revenue that is not rightfully his. I do not believe the amount involved is very large after all. Perhaps the minister can tell us why it should cost from 10 to 40 per cent to sell postage stamps? It seems to me an exorbitant amount for the business done.
The major part of the salaries of country postmasters is paid by commission on the sale of stamps.
Then we will remember that in the estimates.

If a country postmaster were selling revenue stamps for the Customs department he would only get paid really a commission on such sales, while in the other case he is paid in a measure for handling the

mail as well by a percentage commission on the sale of postage stamps. In the city offices where stated salaries of a reasonable amount are paid the vendor of stamps gets I think from one to two per cent.
Has the minister yet the detailed information on the question I asked in reference to the post office printing?
We give our orders to the Printing bureau. The bureau supplies the printing to the postal department. For the most part, if not all, the bureau does the printing itself.
Does the postal department arrange for its own printing outside of the Printing bureau?
No. The practice is for the postal printing to be handed to the Printing bureau. The only order given outside direct by the postal department was for a convention programme.

My information is that some of the post office printing is done outside of the Printing bureau. With the exception of these convention programmes does the minister state that all the printing for the postal department is done either through the Printing bureau or by the latter arranging it to be done outside?
That is my information.

Would the minister make some further investigation on that point? Of course, my information may be incorrect, but I am informed that some printing is done on the order of the Post Office Department outside of the Printing bureau.
What is it?
Are all money orders printed through the Printing bureau?
That is what I thought my hon. friend had in mind. I am informed that the printing of money orders is done through the Printing bureau and not direct by the postal department.

I should certainly like to support the suggestion that revenue stamps be put upon cheques and receipts, but I think it would be a great mistake to compel the public to put a two-cent postage stamp and a one-cent revenue stamp upon letters. Such a regulation would lead to no end of inconvenience, would arouse a lot of adverse criticism throughout the country, and would not secure the information that we have been seeking. If you had revenue stamps on

Supply-Post Office
cheques and receipts, and restricted postage stamps to letters, the department could take one-third of the revenue from postage stamps and treat it a3 belonging to the Department of Customs, which would give us the information we are after now. But I am sure the public would view with disfavour any suggestion of having to put a two-cent stamp of one variety and a one-cent stamp of another variety upon every letter for delivery outside of their own town.

I agree with my hon.
friend that such a regulation would be objectionable. The revenue stamp tax as we may call it could be kept separate, but I do not think it would be advisable to divide the postage of letters.

The reason I interjected my observation was because I rather thought the suggestion of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) was that a man might go to the wicket of a post office and buy one hundred two-cent stamps of one variety and one-hundred one-cent stamps of another variety, and I presumed his idea was that the purchaser would put a two-cent stamp and a one-cent stamp of each variety on his letters. That is what I want to protest against. It would lead to no end of inconvenience, and I am satisfied it would not prove popular.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman does small credit to the common sense of the member for CorOox-Alberni if he thinks that that is what I suggested.
What objection is there to following the British method in regard to stamps, a method which has been in use for such a long period?
What is the English practice?
They have a revenue stamp for revenue purposes, and a postage stamp for postal purposes.

That is really what I think the Minister of Customs is endeavouring to get, so that he will have his revenue absolutely separated from the revenue of the Post Office Department. When the Postmaster General returns I imagine that the customs collector will call upon him the same afternoon concerning this matter, as he has been pressing quite hard to have some new arrangement adopted to accomplish this purpose.

I understand
from my hon. friend that the Postmaster
General is returning home. When is he expected?

The Prime Minister intimated the other night that the Postmaster General would not be back until after the middle of May. In his present state of health his doctor is very doubtful if he will be able to return even then.
The whole result is that nothing will be done, because you cannot pass any legislation after the House prorogues.
I will try to get something done before that time.

As this matter has nothing whatever to do with postal administration, it is hardly a good excuse to shelve it until the Postmaster General comes back. This has nothing to do with the postal service; it relates to special taxation, and I do not see why the matter should stand until the return of the Postmaster General-which means simply shelving it. I hope that, as the Minister of Customs suggests, an effort will be made to put our accounts in more businesslike shape. Not only is it the fact that when but one stamp was necessary for cheques the volume of income attributable to the sale of stamps for other than postal services was negligible compared to what it is now, but in the case of banks and other corporations the stamps were for the most part embossed on the cheques, so that the accounts could be properly kept.
That was not done in the majority of cases, though.
Yes, in the case of the majority of banks.
But the public did not buy them.

Very largely,
yes. I noticed also that through the amendment of the Minister of Customs provision is made for Mr. Anderson. That of course, means that Mr. Anderson's employment is not subject to the Civil Service Act. Has my hon. friend not overlooked many other names that ought to be added if he desires to have the department run in conformity with the law? Over a year ago a vacancy occurred in the postmastership at Woodbridge. About a month afterwards an appointment was made by the Civil Service Commission to fill the vacancy, but that appointment has never been confirmed by the government, and an outsider from Toronto has been brought in to do the work. My hon. friend knows
Supply-Post Office

that is illegal-or is the department to be administered without respect to law? I am not referring to the matter from the point of view of patronage; I am simply dealing with the question whether the Post Office Department is above the law. My hon. friend will find that in not less than twenty-three other cases appointments were properly made by the Civil Service Commission and just as regularly, for political reasons, disregarded. Now the thing is.being legalized in the case of Mr. Anderson; why should the minister not also legalize it at Woodbridge and in connection with these other offices? I would like to know from what votes the payments to these persons are made and who in the department is responsible for them. Under the act it is an offence for any payment to be made in such cases after the expiration of six months. The Postmaster General has managed to get rid of officers who were doing very good work. He has managed to get rid of the former chief inspector, of a very efficient deputy, Mr. Coulter; and apparently, from what was said in the House last night, he is managing to get at outs with a very competent official of the department, Mr. Lemaire. My hon. friend may find it difficult, therefore, to pick up the scattered threads and determine just how these matters stand, but for a commencement I would ask him to give me the date of the appointment by the Civil Service Commission of the postmaster at Woodbridge.

Last evening arguments were advanced in favour of increasing the remuneration of rural mail carriers and establishing new rural mail routes. As a last clincher to the argument one hon. member said: "We have a surplus and can afford to do it." Every well-posted citizen knows that that is beside the fact. I suggest, therefore, that the Minister of Customs and Exuse (Mr. Bureau) make a ruling that excise stamps shall be used on cheques, notes and other documents.
Mr. BLTRF.AU: It is a question of legislation, not of ruling.

If it can be done, whether by legislation or by ruling, let it be done. I have received letters from people who wanted to get the contract for rural mail delivery at less than was being paid for the existing contract. A great deal has been said here by way of comparing conditions in Canada with those in the United States. I would like to know how man}' holidays hon. members would want the rural mail carriers to have, whether five, seven or nine We who live in rural sections know that there are more days than 
that on which the people in rural districts do not get their mail each year owing to the roads being made impassable by storms. The mail carrier, for instance, does not carry the mail on Christmas Day or New Year's Day, and if a great storm comes up between one of these holidays and the ensuing Sunday the people living in the rural sections would not get their mail for several days. These are actual facts. It is better for the mail carrier to work when the _roads are good than when the roads are bad. I was very well acquainted with the man who had control of the rural mail delivery system in Minnesota, and he informed me that there were several days in each year when delivery of mail was impossible on account of severe storms, the breaking up of the roads, and so on. It is the same in northern New England but there are no holidays.
If the mail carriers were to be granted all the legal holidays, as some hon. members have advocated we would be in a fine predicament because there are people living in these back sections who occasionally have some business to do. They may occasionally receive a lawyer's letter giving them perhaps one or two days to pay, or maybe a notice from their bank. That is something that these kind-hearted members who spoke last night in favour of this profligate use of our public money might well consider. We know that all municipal taxes throughout this great country and the United States have doubled and trebled of recent years, and it is because of this wishy-washy way of doing business, of bonusing people, giving them holidays and letting them out of a contract and get more money. In the United States with its much denser population there are ten more patrons to the mile of rural mail routes than there are in this country. We have many rural mail routes that never should have been established. There are instances where a mail carrier is driving on a spur road two or three miles and back. There is nothing like that in the United States. In that country if people live on a spur line they must come down to the main line if they want to get their mail. I only mention these facts because there seems to be quite a mix-up in the ideas of some hon. gentlemen regarding the rural mail delivery system.
May I ask if my hon. friend has any spur line in his riding?
I have.
Of two or three miles in length?
I certainly have.

I have been trying to get one or two and could not succeed.

Supply-Post Office

They were established in my county in 1915. There are a great many routes costing this country altogether too much. In my county there were mail routes running practically across the county that cost not more than six or seven hundred dollars and that are now costing more than six or seven thousand dollars and serving the same people. Many of these rural communities that are being served by the rural mail service would be glad to have it abolished and go back to the little post office. A great many queer things happen in some cases. Certain little kitchen post offices were left, and post offices that were well conducted, housed in a public building in a community where there were two or three churches, and where business was being done, were obliterated because some postmaster may have voted for reciprocity in 1911.
I congratulate you on your influence.
I was a postmaster and mail carrier for thirty-six years, so I have some knowledge of handling the mails.
Perhaps the minister can now give me the information I asked him for.
The officer is not here at the moment. I have not the data, but I think my hon. friend would know it.
I should like to get it on Hansard. There are twenty-three other cases I want to take up with my hon. friend.
There are not twenty-three cases.
Then the appointments must have been straightened out recently.

These cases are only temporary. They arise because of conflict between the Post Office Department and the Civil Service Commission as to their nominee. Out of the hundreds of appointments to post offices, large and small, and until recently they all came under the Civil Service Commission, speaking from memory there are only twelve or thirteen appointments outstanding now. That is not a very large proportion.
The date of the certificate issued by the commission was the 29th of June, 1922. Take the case of Woodbridge. I am not going into details. The commission have absolute power to make that appointment, and eventually their nominee if they do not change their mind will have to be the man appointed. In
the meantime there is a temporary man placed in charge of the post office at Wood-bridge. The contention of the department is that both being returned soldiers the man named by the department having had postal experience is the better qualified for this position. Personally, I do not know, but that is the contention of the department, and they hope to be able to convince the Civil Service Commission that they are right. As a matter of fact, the commission has the authority and their judgment must eventually prevail if they cannot be convinced that it would be wiser to name the other man.

I would like to ask my hon. friend how long he thinks these vacancies should stand. I want to point out some things to him. The act provides that temporary appointments may be made for six months. That is the limitation imposed by the act. Now these vacancies have stood a good deal longer than six months. At Wood-bridge the temporary man who was put in there was brought up from Toronto. I quite admit that they are both returned men, but I would ask my hon. friend whether he does not think in connection with these country post offices that the appointment should go, as it always did in the past, to a resident of the village? Or does he think a man should be brought in from outside? That is what is being done. There is no possible excuse why the law should not be complied with unless it is that the Postmaster General of this country says that he puts himself above the law. There is no good having any half measures here. What is the use of having criminal statutes if ministers of the Crown act with cynical indifference to the laws that are supposed to bind them? Is it simply because the hon. gentleman is in the position of trust that he now occupies that he is to be regarded as above the law? Should he not rather be the first to show others that the law ought to be respected? Does not my hon. friend think so? The people of that place had the right to have the law observed and that appointment made. I would ask my hon. friend how it is that the cheques for payment have been able to be smuggled past the Auditor General, because under the act payments are only allowed to be made for these temporary purposes for six months? What is my hon. friend paying these temporary men, and where is the money coming from? What officer of his is certifying to these payments?

The Civil Service Commission, as I understand it, does not take the extreme view that my hon. friend has announced just now. I do not think there is
Supply-Post Office

any law being violated. I would not like to refer to the Auditor General as my hon. friend has done. I do not think anything can be smuggled by the Auditor General of this country.	.
Who is the Auditor General of this country?
Well then, the Auditor General's office. If my hon. friend thinks that is the case, he should go after the officials of that department.
Oh no, the certificate would come from this department.
My hon. friend did not say that. He said it was being smuggled past the Auditor General.
I said nothing of the kind.
All right, Hansard will show.

What I said, and Hansard will show it, was that I would like to know who the official is who is supposed to see the law carried out but is certifying to these payments so that they can get past the Auditor General.

I do not think there is any question of smuggling names or cooking accounts. It cannot be possible, I do not think there is anything of the kind. There has never been any question as to any of these payments in the case of this office or other offices similarly circumstanced. As I understand it, rural postmasters are not regarded with the same strictness, in the matter of the six months' limit, as perhaps other civil servants are, because the Civil Service Commission readily understands the difficulties surrounding the appointment of these officers as distinguished from those that are appointed to the inside service.
I think that before the item passes my hon. friend should bring down the papers showing exactly how these payments are made. My hon. friend says that the general act does not apply to the postmaster.
I did not say so.
I so understood my hon. friend.
You understood wrongly.

Then I am very happy to be corrected. If the general act does apply we have no right to make any of these payments 'after the expiration of the 
six months, and we are entitled to know therefore how they could be made. Consequently, as the minister does not say that the act does not apply, I will ask him to bring down the papers showing how these payments are made.
I will bring down the papers. In the meantime we can continue with the item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I will have to ask that it stand until the information for which I asked has been brought down.
There are other hon. members who doubtless wish to discuss the item; my. hon. friend is not the only one who has the right.
The Chairman asked whether the item should carry. I have no objection to anybody else discussing it, none whatever.
Go on and discuss it then.

The ,minister seemed to think that somebody else wanted the floor and, of course, I should be very pleased to yield the floor, or anything else, to my hon. friend at any time. I notice we are having an increase in the staff.
No, a reduction.

A reduction, is it? That is splendid. In the general total there is a reduction, but I notice that in some instances there are changes
5 p.m. in the numbers. Has my hon. friend any particulars to give as to that? Is there anything he lays any claim to in connection with that as to economy or the like?
Yes.
In which case?

In the whole. There is an abolition of sixteen positions and the creation of eight positions with smaller salaries, a reduction of eight officials, although there have been some increases in salary, statutory and otherwise, there is a decrease in the whole amount of $2,000.
Just while we are on the question of totals, will my hon. friend give the receipts of the department up to the end of the year?
I think that should be gross receipts.
It is gross receipts.
If it is then was my hon. friend right when he said that more stamps would be sold. It was stamps issued, was it.
Yes, issued.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Before the item carries I want to know exactly how the regular practice which _ has been referred to is being carried on in this department. It may be that when the information comes down we will find there is nothing irregular, there may be some extraordinary explanation of it, but at present there is what, on the face of it, is a confession that the law is absolutely disregarded in connection with the Woodbridge post office. My hon. friend says the law is disregarded in connection with some eleven other post offices and he says it is a very small number. I think my hon. friend will find there are more cases than the eleven which he admits.
I will tell my hon. friend the exact number.

The details show a decrease of something over $2,000. Will the minister tell us the amount of the superannuation allowance in the case of the former deputy minister and the former superintendent of postal services because, I think, if these two items are added the decrease becomes an increase. I want to say that in superannuating these gentlemen the government has got rid of the two most experienced and best qualified postal officers in the Dominion, men who are just as capable of doing the work they formerly did as they ever were and perhaps a little more so. Instead of trying to promote economy it looks as though the Postmaster General were trying to put a friend into a lucrative position; under the guise of a superannuation the government have practically dismissed the former deputy 'minister and his chief assistant, the postal superintendent. If you add the superannuation in each case to the expenditure it will show an increase instead of a decrease. And this is done by a government that makes some sort of spurious claim to be economical.
My hon. friend asked for the retiring allowance. Dr. Coulter receives $4,200 and Mr. Ross $3,900.
That is over $8,000?	_

My hon. friend must remember that both these gentlemen paid a certain amount into the superannuation fund. Their retirement would not involve any charge at all upon the post office; the fund from which that is taken is a different one altogether. If my hon. friend's argument were correct we might take the whole list of superannuations that have taken place in connection with the department and charge the expense against the Post Office Department. Both of these gentlemen asked for their retirement and it was granted.
Is there correspondence to show that?
I have a. c8py of Dr. Coulter's letter. I have already read it.
Frozen out.
Did Mr. Ross ask for his superannuation ?
I am informed so. I have read Dr. Coulter's letter.
I would like to see the letter brought down.
Which letter?
Mr. Ross.
We will get copies of them both.

I do not think the acting minister seriously wants to let the House understand that either of these gentlemen got out voluntarily. I do not think the Postmaster General, if he were here, would say so. I think the minister would take the responsibility for bringing about their retirement, rightly or wrongly-he would claim, of course, rightly. But the fact undoubtedly is, unless I am very much misinformed, that the minister came to the conclusion that they should be out, and then he proceeded to get their resignations, their requests for retirement. They came. Of the fact I do not want to speak at first hand knowledge; but I feel so convinced that that is the case, that I do not think the minister should seek to give the House the other impression. There are circumstances when such a course is justified, That I am not discussing for the moment; but I object to the House being given the impression that these men wanted to get out of the service, and that they came forward
Supply-Post Office

themselves and forced themselves out. I am quite certain that is not the case. The minister is talking around the subject when he says that they paid into the retirement fund and became entitled to the $4,200 and the $3,900. That is correct, and the amount is not charged against the Post office Department, but it comes out of the country. If they were in the service, they would not be getting that. They would be getting the salaries that the new men are getting, and the country would be saved this $8,100 until the time came for them to retire. Therefore, what the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Hocken) says is absolutely right. Instead of being ahead, the country is behind just the difference between the $8,100 and the $2,000. Is it not a fact that Mr. Hector Verret has been retired?
Some time ago, I think.
But by the present minister within the last fiscal year?

I think the position was
abolished by the Griffenhagens.

That would be a very
good thing. That would be a contraction. I see this does not appeal to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe).
It certainly does.

Everything except an
expansion is a joke to him.
Some contractions are.
There is nobody, I understand, in Mr. Verret's place?
I was informed the position is abolished.

I hope the government
does not undo that piece of good work that was done by the late government, although I am really apprehensive that it will, and get somebody in there. As regards those two gentlemen, they have been relieved of their duties by the will of the minister, with the result that the country is out at least $6,100.

Has there been any change in the policy of the department respecting what we have been calling spur lines? As I understand the matter, what is meant is this. A carrier has to go two or three miles up the line and has to double and come back. If there has been a change, I should like to secure one or two extra services in the county of Simcoe. I note that the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Baldwin) said that in his constituency he had a number of those. I

congratulate him; he has done good work for his patrons in his constituency, and I would like to do the same for mine.
Another matter I should like to bring forward is this. I do not want the department to do for me anything that is not being done for others. I have five farmers on a route, and the furthest one happens to be within a mile from where the carrier passes on the highway. I understand there is a rule of the department that they will not serve any man who is not a mile away, even if he is on a spur. The result is that these five men have to walk, perhaps in very stormy weather, all the way from a quarter of a mile to seven' eighths of a mile to the comer, and there they may have to wait half an hour or an hour on a bad day for the carrier to come along. A change of that kind would not be very expensive. I suppose there are many such instances; but if that sort of thing is being done in other ridings, and there has been a change in policy, we should all know of it, because I have no doubt that every member has cases of this kind, and it is not right that some should be successful in their efforts to secure relief while that relief is denied to others.

I imagine the same policy applies as far as practicable to all communities. There may be certain circumstances surrounding particular communities where the population is very dense, where there may be an exception; but I know of none, and I know of no change in policy. Surely in the older sections it is not cruel to ask a man to walk nearly a mile when there are in this country so many sections where people have to drive seven or eight miles to get their mail. I do not think any exceptional treatment is being given.

The mail route of which I spoke before was established in the summer of 1915 against all overtures of mine and everything that I could do myself to prevent its being established, not by this government., but by the late government. That is in connection with what I said about a postmaster being dismissed for having voted for reciprocity in 1911.
What is causing the delay in appointing a deputy minister for the department and in filling the other position of superintendent?
As a matter of fact, I am not in a position to say what is causing the delay. I would presume that it is the illness of the minister more than anything else.

What is the cause of that?

Supply-Post Office
Is it the delay that is causing the minister's illness, or the minister's illness that is causing the delay?

I might as well make it
clear that there is no question of the minister's illness and serious illness. I would not want any of the members to be led to believe that there was not a serious condition of health existing with the Postmaster General. I know that to be true.

It is a very serious thing that a department of this kind should run along so far and through the session of this House without any responsible person in charge, without any person who knows the department to represent it in this House. There is no deputy minister to come and advise the acting minister about anything connected with the department. That is a serious thing and some effort should be made to fill these positions. Perhaps the acting minister can appoint a deputy.

The acting minister will not do that. I will call my hon. friend's attention to this fact, that he was quite contented, in times gone by, to have a minister who never came into this House. The Postmaster General was then in the Senate. No person regrets more than I do the absence of the Postmaster General.
He had a deputy minister.
As good Samaritans do in a government or elsewhere, whoever is able does his best to carry the burden of the absent one.
Does the minister have any hopes of being relieved of either the Militia department or the Railway department in the near future, and if so, which one? He ought to know about that.
My. right hon. friend is really asking too much.
The minister will, perhaps, give us the list he has of post offices held up.
There were twenty. My hon. friend was nearly right. Since the list was made, postmasters appointed by the commission have taken charge of five.
When were the appointments made?
I will hand my hon. friend the list I have.
Then I suppose this can be put on Hansard without wasting the time of the committee in reading it.

It has already been
brought down as a return.
Get a ruling on it.
The right hon. the leader of the Opposition moved for it one day in the absence of some other hon. member, I forget whom. At any rate it has been brought down.
I notice from it that my hon. friend has apparently obeyed the law in connection with the five cases. Am I right in that assumption?

I would not put it that
way.	,
That would be too frank.
Would it not be true?

I would not go so far because I want to be accurate, and I do not want to admit even tacitly that I broke the law. I would say, that, as in all cases, investigations are proceeding and communications are being exchanged, and the department after conference and due consideration have given instructions for the postmasters, to whom certificates were issued by the Civil Service Commission, to take their places in these five instances. As a matter of fact it is only a question of time, unless the commission changes its mind, when the same thing must be done in connection with all cases, because the power eventually rests with the commission.
Am I to understand that the cases against which the minister has a mark are the ones in which the law has been carried out?
I would not put it that way.
Are these the cases in which the appointments made by the commission have been made effective?

I stated the matter
clearly.
No.

Well, to the average person. I explained that in these five cases, after conference and investigation, the department had given instructions for the persons to whom the Civil Service Commission had

Supply-Post Office

issued certificates to be placed in charge of the offices.
Would my hon. friend conceive it to be the duty of a minister to carry out the appointments made by the Civil Service Commission under the act?

It would be the duty of a minister to see that the laws governing his department were carried out; and unless the minister or the department can convince the commission that its appointee is not the best qualified person for the office in question, then eventually the minister must acquiesce in the appointment of the commission.
Another question. In the minister's view, how long a time has a minister the right to hang up these appointments?
My hon. friend, lawyerlike, is of course getting down to the crossquestioning.
Not at all; I am merely trying to get the facts, that is all.
I would not say that my hon. friend was trying to get the facts; he is trying to elicit opinions.
I am asking your opinion.
Well, you know, opinions are not evidence. My hon. friend is not trydng to get the facts.
I am going to the statutes, but you do not like statutes.

Of course, my opinion I can give for what it is worth. Circumstances differ and each case has to be dealt with on its merits, and as the responsible head of the department views those merits. Conditions might arise in one case that wmuld not at all obtain in the other, and the information necessary to be submitted to the commission might be more easily obtainable in one case than in another. My view, as I have already expressed it, is that eventually the Civil Service Commission, if it adheres to a nominee of its own, must make the appointment, as it has the right to do under the act. But in order that the public may be served as efficiently as possible, and that the machinery of government, not only of the departments but of the Civil Service Commission as well, might work smoothly, I think, the commission act fairly in allowing a reasonable time in which to see whether information cannot be placed before them which might lead them to view the

situation as the Post Office Department views it.

I wonder whether my hon. friend can tell me what investigation is going on at Woodbridge? He says that when the investigation is over the appointment will be made unless the Civil Service Commission changes it mind. Well, what investigation is now going on?
I would not care to give the details.

Surely my hon. friend knows there are none. He must Certainly know that nothing has been done, but that there has been a mere refusal by the minister to carry out the law. Nothing has been done in connection with the thing for months, and if the minister wants to say now, as a matter of fact, that an investigation is going on, then I would ask for the details.

Further inquiries are being made. Now that my hon. friend has asked so many questions, showing that he has no confidence in the acting minister or in the department and being evidently under the impression that we are smuggling things by, I might inform him that I have given instructions to hasten to a conclusion as rapidly as possible some of these positions which he says are being hung up. I do not think that anything can be gained by hurrying too rapidly, and personally I should like to know all the circumstances. Now, I could relate some circumstances about Woodbridge.
Go on.

But that would not help the situation there; and I could do the same in regard to a good many others. That, however, is not my province. I want to get matters cleared up as rapidly as possible and that is what I purpose doing. I do not want to say anything further until I get all the information I want.

Assuming that the Civil Service Commission has appointed a postmaster at Woodbridge, is it the function of the minister, not merely to examine into the qualifications of the appointee, but also to nominate someone else for the appointment, giving reasons therefor?
No, I would not go that length. In the case of Woodbridge the man is in charge now who was in charge when the certificate was issued to the other man.

The position is temporary.

Supply-Post Office
It can only be temporary. He has been there now since the certificate was issued to the other man.
He has been there a year.
It does not make any difference how long he has been there. The other man's certificate was issued in June, 1922, and that is quite a while ago.
How can he be kept in the position for more than six months?
He has been kept in it and paid.
Illegally.

I do not think the commission complies strictly with the act in regard to this six months' provision, in the case of the outside service. I do not think that is their practice. However, these matters will be cleared up in due course, and I want to see it done in all these cases and see the occupants of the positions made permanent as nearly as possible.

The point I am getting at is simple. Members of parliament to-day are not permitted-at least that is the understanding-to make recommendations to the Civil Service Commission as to who they think should be appointed as postmasters or in any other capacity. I take that to be the law; at least it is what is generally understood to be the practice, the object being to preclude patronage. Now, is it a fact, with reference to these twenty or any one of them, that the minister of the department recommends to the commission some person in lieu of an appointee whom the commission has already recommended? Is that the practice now, or has it been done in any case? If it has, it seems to me perfectly clear that the most powerful person is endeavouring to exercise patronage. and induce the Civil Service Commission to make other appointments that do not seem to be in compliance with the law.
Read the evidence before the committee. It is to the contrary.
There is nothing to hinder my hon. friend making a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission, but that does not mean that his nominee would be appointed: he might be or he might not.

I understood it was not proper for us to do so. I am glad to know that it is proper.

You will find the Civil Service Commission receives recommendations from all sorts of persons; I know the department does. When a vacancy occurs an inspector of the department places a person in charge temporarily until such time as the Civil Service Commission makes its selection. In this case the department, rightly or wrongly has differed with some of the nominees of the Civil Service Commission on information that the department has. But the occupancy of the position by any person other than the commisioners' appointee is and can only be temporary, and eventually, if the Civil Service Commission does not change its viewpoint, its nominee is the proper person for the vacancy and must be appointed.

If what the minister says is carried to its logical conclusion it merely means that the intent of the act is defeated. The Civil Service Commission makes the appointment to the position. The government have the power to refuse that appointment. They would be justified in refusing to confirm it if, on the appointment being notified to them, they knew of circumstances that in their judgment disqualified the appointee, in which event it would be the duty of the government, I think, simply to transmit those circumstances to the commission. That would not involve any delay at all, would be carrying out the spirit of the act, and would be as far as the government in any case would be justified in going. If, on the other hand, after the Civil Service Commission makes an appointment, the government set to work to find whether the appointee is going to suit them from all standpoints, and they have an investigation themselves over the action of the commission, and they have a temporary man continued and continued temporarily in the position until they get through with their investigation, that is simply defeating the act. The word "eventually" means nothing; the word "temporary" means very little. Temporary employment may be for ten years. The act provides for six months, but six months should not be necessary. The duty of the government to install a man at once, unless they know of circumstances, not political, that they believe have not been brought to the mind of the commission, in which event they would be right in transmitting the information. Beyond that they have not any right to go ahead conducting prolonged investigations in review of the work of the Civil Service Commission. I think that is a fair statement of the position. If the government just go far enough in the exercise
Supply-Post Office

of the prerogative that the minister says they have, why, they might just as well recommend the repeal of the act. Putting a man in a vacancy in the first place, and keeping him there until the government is satisfied after their own investigation of the recommendation of the commission, is simply repealing the act.
It ought to be repealed anyway.
I understood my hon. friend is going to bring down the pay sheets showing just how these temporary employees are paid. It may be that they can be paid legally under the act, but I do not think so.

I have not made any
promise to bring down the pay sheets. My hon. friend wanted to know how we "smuggled" in those pay sheets. That was the word he used. I insisted that they were not "smuggled." He asked by whose authority payments were made and I told him I would get the information. I do not propose to bring down all the pay sheets.
I only want a sample.
I will bring down the information I promised to clear his mind. In the meantime we might as well go on discussing the item, because I suppose there will be a discussion on it.
I do not believe any one wishes to discuss it further. I suppose this statement from the minister is to go in Hansard?
It will have to be read if it is to go in Hansard, unless unanimous consent is given for it to be taken as read.
I am willing to have it go in Hansard.

If the hon. gentleman wants it read I have pleasure in complying with his wishes. This, then, Mr. Chairman, is a list of post office appointments which have been hung up by the hon. Postmaster General. The first column contains the names of the post offices, the second column the names of the commission's nominees, the third column their military status, and the fourth column the names of the temporary incumbents. Bearing this description in mind, I now read the list. The first place is Alexandria, Ontario; the commission has appointed Mr. W. A. Morrison; his military [Mr. Meighen.l	I
status is O.A.S.; the Postmaster General maintains Mr. Peter Ferguson in Mr. Morrison's place.	,
What does O.A.S. mean?
My hon. friend will have to ask the minister; I am reading his own list.
Overseas active service.
The next place is St. Barnabe Nord, P.Q.; the commission's nominee is Mr. J. N. Gelinas-
How do you spell that name?
Capital G-e-1-i-n-a-s.
Go on. I know about that case; it is all right too.

Mr. Gelinas'
position is held by a nominee of the Postmaster General, Mr. Charles Marcouiller. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would like me to spell that name?
Yes.
I suggest that my hon. friend is not reading the document; he is editing it.
If my hon. friend is objecting to my method of reading I am quite ready to change it.
Put the document in Hansard.

Mr. Chairman, may we
comment on this as the hon. gentleman proceeds?
Yes.
Yes.

This man Gelinas bought out the place from his predecessor, Gelinas. I was informed of it. I said that even though under the old administration it was the custom to barter post office or other government jobs I would not stand for it. Thereupon Mr. Marcouiller was chosen and appointed by the Civil Service Commission. There are the facts.
Then the return is all wrong; it does not show how the department acted.
You are reading it upside down.
I am reading the statement as I received it from the Acting Postmaster General.
Leave out the editing and get it right-read it.
Here it is. The commission's nominee is stated to be J. N. Gelinas. My hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) says they did not appoint him, they appointed Charles Marcouiller.

They appointed him and then dismissed him when they found he was bartering a public office.
* Sir HENRY DRAYTON: Who is there
now?
Marcouiller.
He is there-[DOT]
And he is going to stay. He has the sanction of the Civil Service Commission.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I am going to ask my friend if he will not bring down a statement that gives us the facts-
Go on with your reading.
-because the facts are incorrectly stated here apparently.

No, the facts are correctly stated, Mr. Chairman. The Civil Service Commission, through their inspector, Mr. Green, recommended this man Gelinas. I went to the Postmaster General and told him that it would not do to barter these public offices. He agreed with me, and the Civil Service Commission confirmed the appointment of Mr. Marcouiller. He was recommended by the department at my instance, he is there and is going to stay there, and he is going to give good service too.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this is only another tribute to the tremendous power and influence of my hon. friend.
My power is due to honesty. The straight course is always the shortest.

The next post office on the list is that of Field, B.C. The commission appointed Mr. J. Roberts, whose status is " O.A.S.". The nominee of the Postmaster General is Mrs. F. Howatson. The next is St. Moise Station, P.Q. The commission's nominee is Mrs. A. L. Michaud; the Postmaster General's nominee is Mrs. S- Vail-lancourt. The next is St. Phillippe d'Argen-teuil, P.Q.; the commission's nominee is Mr. T. LaMarche; the Postmaster General's man is Osias Laurin.

Is he in or out?

He is in; he is the Postmaster General's man. The next is Portneuf, P.Q. The commission appointed to that office Mr. Joseph Thibault, who has military status. The Postmaster General's man is Mr. Isidore Marcotte.
What is the revenue from that office?

The hon. member will have to ask the minister. The next is the post office at Maddington Falls, P.Q. The commission have appointed to that office Mr. Emilien Rivard, who has military status. Evidently there is a family quarrel here, because the minister's nominee is the wife of the commission's nominee. The next is Clements-port, N.B. The commission's nominee is Mr. H. G. Potter, who has military status; the Postmaster General's nominee is Captain Elias Rawding.	.
Did my hon. friend say that was in New Brunswick?
Yes.
That is another mistake.

status; his position is held by Miss L. G. Shannon, Kenabeek, Ont.; commission's nominee, Mr. J. E. Irwin; his place is held by Mr. James Enright, St. John N.B.; commission's nominee, Mr. A. W. Lingley; his duties are performed by the postmaster and other employees in charge of staffs, as shown by the return. I point out, Mr. Chairman, a situation which I do not think so many of my hon. friends will laugh at; out of this long list, the gentlemen appointed by the Civil Service Commission all hold military status, whereas of the appointees of the Postmaster General but one holds military status.
Who appointed Mr. Lingley in St. John?
He has been appointed by the commission but he has not been given the position.
My hon. friend did not read all this document.
You said I was a bad reader, and I stopped.

Instructions have been issued for the transfer of Blackville, Portsmouth, tVardner, Tamworth and Marmora post offices to the commission's nominees, but the transfers have not yet been reported to the department.
Now, that is very important. Of these post offices my hon. friend has named, five have been handed over to the commission's nominees. That should have been read and put in the record.

My hon. friend said that before.
Mr. GRAHAM [DOT] My hon. friend was reading this document and putting it on Hansard, and he left out a very important item, namely, that, of the twenty offices mentioned, twenty-five per cent have already been placed in charge of the commission's nominees. So that this document, without further comment, must be discounted twenty-five per cent. Moreover, it bears out what I have already stated: you cannot make appointments to all these offices in rural districts on the basis of the rule of three. I said a few moments ago that, information was being secured in respect to all these different cases, and that as rapidly as possible we were filling the positions, where the commission changed its mind, according to the commission's nominee. Twenty-five per cent of that has been done-yes, more, the commission changed its mind in connection with the post office to which my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) has referred. I contend that, in connection with appointments to these
TSir Henry Drayton.]
offices the department has been doing very well; very few are at this moment not in the hands of the nominee of the Civil Service Commission and such as are not are being placed there. But in some instances the commission has changed its mind after getting all the facts. As I said before, if the commission does not change its mind after all the objections are presented, its nominee must stand. In the meantime I maintain that the position of the department is commendable, not attackable, on this point, because it is not an easy matter to handle throughout the whole Dominion of Canada.
Why was the. Portsmouth appointment held up? There was no sale of that post office.
That appointment is now in the hands of the nominee of the Civil Service Commission.
But why was it held up so long? I can understand delay where there is a question of the post office being sold, but there was no such question in this case.

There were strenuous representations made to the department that this post office should be put in a separate building, also that it should be kept in its present location. The suitability of the commission's nominee was also questioned and the department investigated the matter, just as it does in a great many other cases. That is the report I have. The department having investigated the matter asked that the commission's nominee be put in the position, and that was done.
He is a good man. There is no dispute about that. I know him.

Item agreed to.
Post Office-outside service-to provide for the payment of salary at the rate of $1,000 a year to Lucien Pacaud as the representative of the ^Canadian government on the Pacific Cable board, as from January 16, 1923, $208.33
To pay J. W. Paddle, postmaster at Sunset lake, Saskatchewan, and mail contractor on the Spalding and Sunset lake route, for the loss of a horse while conveying the mail on October 6, 1922, $150.
To pay certain employees of the postal service in the Quebec district for extra services in connection with checking incoming and outgoing British mails during the summer of 1922, $288.14.
Is this Mr. Pacaud the assistant of the High Commissioner?
Joint secretary.

This amount is in addition to his salary, of course?

Supply-Post Office
Yes.
What is his salary?
I do not know. That would come under the estimates of the Prime Minister for the High Commissioner's office.
It looks as if this was entirely a new matter.
Oh no. The Post Office Department makes this appointment every year, and this year it has appointed Mr. Pacaud.
Who acted before?
Mr. Lang, I think.
Who is Mr. Lang?
He was not in the High Commissioner's office, and it was thought better to have a man from the High Commissioner's office, so Mr. Pacaud was chosen.
With reference to the second item, is it the usual practice to indemnify mail carriers for the loss of their horses on the routes?

I am hardly in a mood to admit anything. We have to take each case on its merits. The inspector made a report on this case, recommending that we might well pay this man $150 for the loss of his horse under all the circumstances, and the department is carrying out his recommendation. I would not say that it would be constituting a precedent, for this reason: Every case will have to be considered on its merits, and if cause is not shown, the department would not be compelled to pay. There have been cases before, I think, where men have been indemnified under similar circumstances.

What I want to get at is this: It is not that the amount is very much, although it is a pretty good price for the horse, but if this vote is passed will the minister give me the assurance that in a similar case the owner will get the same treatment? I lost one of my own, and I could give the details which I think would justify payment.
I would say this, that every case will be dealt with by the department on its merits, and if my hon. friend makes out as good a case as this man, he will have to be paid for his horse.
Might we know what the merits are, so that I might compare my case with this one?

And make the evidence to
suit the case.

This driver lost one of his horses while carrying the mail. We heard a lot last night about the mail carriers and how poorly they are paid. Well, this horse met with an accident and was killed. We had an inspector investigate the circumstances, and he recommended that we ought to pay for the horse. That is the whole case. If my hon. friend presents his case to the department and the inspector, after investigating it, feels that he ought to be compensated, there is no doubt in the world he would be paid.

I suppose it would be all right to present the case here.
Mr, GRAHAM: Oh, no.
I mean the general details. They are practically the same.
What kind of an investigation did the inspector make into this matter.
A post-mortem.
I cannot say exactly what kind of an investigation he held. We have to trust our inspectors and officials. The inspector made his investigation and the department is acting on his recommendation.

Is it not a fact that this mail carrier simply wrote in to the inspector a statement of the case, and on the strength of that letter a report was made without taking any evidence whatever, the inspector simply forwarding the letter to the department with the recommendation that the claim be paid? I understand that those are the circumstances.
I could not say what further investigation the inspector made, but on the evidence that he had he recommends the payment of this amount. What else can the department depend on?
What was the nature of the evidence?

I will read the letter of this mail carrier. I wish some of those members who were so sympathetic towards the mail couriers yesterday were busy here now. Here is a poor mail courier who has lost his horse in this unremunerative work for a hardhearted government, and some hon. gentlemen object to his being compensated for the loss of his horse. His letter reads:
Dear Sir,-I beg to report that the incoming mail of October 6tb to Sunset lake arrived four hours late owing to a serious accident.

One of the mail courier's horses was killed while travelling through a bush trail about two miles from Sunset lake by a pole, which when stepped on one end by the horse flew up and the other end entering the horse's stomach caused death almost instantly.
The delay resulted through effort spent to save the horse and the difficulty of procuring another to complete the trip as the above occurred in a lonely spot.
This horse was a splendid percheron mare and as her value represents more than a full year of mail courier's salary, you will realize what it means to me as I had only three horses before.
Will you kindly forward a request to the General Superintendent of Postal Service, asking him if, under the unfortunate circumstances, some remuneration for this horse can be made as her loss without remuneration will seriously cripple my ability to continue the performance of my mail service as only one of my remaining horses is able to travel on the road and I am at present continuing with a borrowed horse.
Trusting you will give this matter your early consideration and thanking you for the above favor, I am Yours faithfully,
Sgd. J. W. Paddle,
P.M. & Mail Courier.
Now if that statement be true a splendid Percheron mare would be worth more money than an ordinary animal. It is not extravagant therefore to contribute $150 towards the loss which this man has suffered and I submit that it is not establishing a precedent.

I still doubt very much whether this animal was worth $150. I did not attend any horse sales in the West in October but I did in January and I saw good horses-young horses at that just ready to break in-sell for $20. Those were better horses than I have seen on most of the rural mail routes in western Canada, and I think the amount in this case is entirely excessive. I think it should be reduced to at least $75 and I move accordingly.

Shall the resolution

I am not
opposed to this payment because of the amount or because the horse was not worth $150, although knowing the actual district where the accident occurred I should be inclined to doubt whether this very valuable Percheron mare was worth $150 last October. Apart, however, from that the objection in my opinion, is that it is creating a precedent. I think this man took the contract, as was said here last night, at. a figure altogether too low; he probably underbid somebody else in order to get it. I do not know as to that but this I am aware of: This man is carrying the mail 52 times a year, on a round trip of 22 miles, for $125, being $25 less than the figure at which he values the horse. Now, I submit that he should not have used a $150 horse for carrying the mail. Bearing in mind the wear and tear involved, and the other conditions,
[Mr. Graham.l
he would have been better advised to have used a $50 pony to carry the mail at the price he was getting. I want to state that there are scores of mail carriers in that same district, or in similar districts within a couple of hundred miles of it, who are having losses owing to accidents to their horses and they never ask the department to recoup them. They are quite prepared to face the possible consequences when they take the mail contract. I say this would be a dangerous precedent to establish. For example, let me cite the following incident. I happen to know a mail carrier who lost a team of horses not' so far away from this very post office a couple of years ago. It was about this time of yeai and a certain creek was in freshet. His tearr was drowned in trying to ford the creek; the owner thought he had not time to take the bridge which would involve a detour of some 15 or 20 miles. I never heard of any complaint by him. He was making a business of carrying the mail and he took his losses as a matter of course. I know of others who have lost horses under circumstances just as exceptional as these. They sound exceptional but actually they are not so. Just as in all bush countries it is not an uncommon thing for a horse to injure himself

very often fatally-by stepping on a stick. This man knew the conditions, just as other mail carriers know them, because he had often travelled the bush roads. Other men take these chances without any hope of compensation and this man should do the same. I am not going to oppose this item but I must say that it is creating a very dangerous precedent. There will be a great number of other claims made in future, quite as justifiable as the present one, and it would be well to draw the line before it is too late.

Item agreed to.

subtopic: BUFFALO AND FORT ERIE PUBLIC BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
This bill was passed last session in this House; it then went to the Senate and was held up there at the request of the National Railways, who have since withdrawn all opposition. In the meantime, an act on similar lines was passed by the legislature of the state of New York, and there was introduced by the New York legislature a section 16, which is exactly the same as clause IS in this bill, the idea of the company being that it is a public enterprise, undertaken by public-spirited citizens in the state of New York and Ontario, to build this bridge and to carry out the undertaking as regards expenditure. with the idea that the state of New York and the Dominion of Canada, or the province of Ontario, as the case may be, will eventually take over the expenditure or the assets of the company. As regards what my hon. friend says, the bill is not very clear. I cannot, however, see any objection to its going through in this form, because in any case either country would have the power of expropriation as regards its half of the undertaking. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), as one of the promoters of the bill, stated that it was originally intended in 1913 or 1914 to be an undertaking as a memorial to the one hundred years of peace, and that in the meantime the
war intervened. The strongest explanation that I can make is that it was at the request of the joint promoters in New York state and in Canada that this provision was incorporated in the bill, and it was apparently insisted upon by the legislature of the state of New York that it should be so incorporated.

subtopic: BUFFALO AND FORT ERIE PUBLIC BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext: I do not for a moment suggest that the people behind this are not public spirited, that this is not a very desirable thing or that it would not be very useful in that part of the province. Therefore, I want to do all I can to assist the matter; but my hon. friend has not quite answered the inquiry I made. The clause I have quoted provides that when the corporate obligations of the company shall have been paid and its capital stock retired, its property rights and franchises in Canada shall be conveyed to the Dominion or to any province, municipality or agency thereof as the Governor in Council may designate. How can the time ever come when that will be done? It stands to reason that if they want to make a presentation of it to the government they can do so without this clause. I cannot see the purpose of the clause. It does not compel them to hand it over. There are no by-laws at present which say that the stock is to be issued and that stock shall be retired within a certain number of years or by an annual payment. I have done my best to figure out the purpose of the clause, but it seems to me that in its present form it is useless. I suppose it is the same clause as appears in the New York bill, but what good purpose it serves there either I cannot see. It did occur to me that the purpose of the clause was possibly to protect the state of New York on the one hand and Canada on the other, or in other words, that the company could not ask the Dominion of Canada to take over the bridge until its obligation's were paid and its capital stock retired. If that is the purpose of it I certainly do not think that this clause accomplishes it. However, if the chairman himself thinks that the clause is a useful one and protects the country in any way I shall not further oppose it. The chairman heard the further explanation given at the last meeting at which I regret to say I was not present, and so I shall say no more. But I must admit that I do not see what good purpose the clause serves. There are certainly no by-laws now in existence, because there cannot be By-laws of a company that is not incorporated.

Section agreed to.
