Mr. ANDREW McMASTER (Brome) moved the second reading of Bill No. 75 (from the Senate) to make lawful the marriage of a woman to her deceased husband's brother or such brother's son.
He said: This legislation, Mr. Speaker, originated in the Senate, where it was passed with practically no discussion. I do not intend to delay the House at any great length in exposition of the bill, which after all is of a very simple nature. For the last forty years our law has provided that a man may marry his deceased's wife's sister; in other words, that a widower may marry his sister-in-law. But strange to say the inverse is not the case, and the widow cannot marry her brother-in-law. Now it would appear to me that on the most reasonable grounds there is no real distinction or indeed any distinction to be drawn.
It may interest hon. members if I refer for a few moments to the history of the legislation in this parliament upon the subject. In 1880 Mr. Girouard, at that time member for Jacques Cartier county, who, if I mistake not, was afterwards one of the Justices of the Supreme Court, introduced a bill permitting not only the marriage of the man with his deceased wife's sister, but also the marriage of the woman with her deceased husband's brother. The bill was debated at very considerable length and passed by an overwhelming majority. However, the Senate of that day was not composed as the Senate of to-day is, and there the bill met with opposition and was rejected, but by a very small majority. If that measuie had passed there would have been no necessity for the present bill. Two years afterwards Mr. Girouard introduced another bill, in which he asked merely for legislation permitting the marriage of the man with his deceased wife's sister. That bill was debated for some time, it received a large majority in this House, and was also passed by the Senate. Therefore, as I stated at the outset of my observations, for the last forty years a man in Canada has had the right- although he has been under no obligation- in, the event of his wife's death to marry any one of her sisters. But the wife who lost her husband has not had the right to marry his brother.
Now, it would seem to me that if we believe in "equal rights for all and special privileges for none" that men and women in regard to this as in regard to many other matters should be put on the same basis. My first argument in support of the bill is that for the last forty years in which the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
present legislation has been on our statute books I know of no. inconvenience caused by it. I believe if this bill were accepted and we could cast our minds forward for forty years, we would see that no inconvenience would result from the adoption of this legislation.
I am told that the provision under which a woman is forbidden to marry her deceased husband's brother is often disregarded, the marriage taking place in this country, or is often avoided by parties going into the United States-because there is only one state in' that country which forbids such a marriage-there contracting the marriage and returning to Canada if they see fit to do so. I think public opinion is in favour of this bill. When Mr. Girouard brought in his bill of 1882, which is the present legislation, he was able to invite the attention of his colleagues to the fact that three hundred women in Montreal had petitioned for the legislation. I can now tell the House that the Local Council of Women, representing a large body of thoughtful women throughout the country, some 300,000 in number, have asked for this legislation.
There cannot be any objection to this legislation on the part of those who are guided in life by the Scriptures. We will remember that little idyll found in the Book of Ruth which tells us that Naomi said to her daughters-in-law that they should go home because she was unable to provide them with husbands in the country to which she was returning. In the old days-if we are to have recourse to those early times for enlightenment and example-it was not only the right but the obligation of the male survivors of a deceased husband to marry the widow. You will remember that the founder of the House of David, before he married Ruth, received his right to do so from a nearer relation. So that I think we need not have any religious qualms in accepting this legislation. It seems to me so reasonable and so equitable as to really not require any argument, and I shall reserve anything further I may have to say in the case of any opposition being made to the bill. It seems to me that the bill speaks for itself.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure) in the chair.
Trade and Commerce-Commercial Intelligence Service, including salaries, travelling expenses, contingencies and other expenditure of Trade Commissioners,
Assistant Trade Commissioners, Junior Trade Commissioners and Commercial Agents; and miscellaneous expenses in connection with the development and extension of Canadian trade, $320,000.

How many trade commissioners have we, and what are the principal countries in which they are located?
Mr./ROBB:	We have twenty-three trade
commissioners and four commercial agents. The trade commissioners are located at Melbourne, Cape Town, London, Manchester, Glasgow, Shanghai, Liverpool, Hamburg, Rotterdam, Milan, Buenos Aires, Yokohama, Barbados, Auckland, Paris, Calcutta, Brussels, Rio de Janeiro, New York, Singapore, Jamaica and Havana, Bristol, Mexico City. The commercial agents are located at Sydney, Australia; Christiania, Norway; Nassau, Bahamas, and Port of Spain, Trinidad.

There has been a good
deal of talk in the press at times about our dommercial agents, or the lack of them. Would the minister state what are their general duties and what success they are having so far as this country is concerned?

The duties of the trade commissioners are to look after trade generally, to keep in touch with the conditions in the countries in which they are located, to discover what products Canada may with profit ship to those countries, to keep in their offices a register of exporting firms who desire to do business, to advise the business people of the country where they are located as to what goods might be purchased in Canada, and generally speaking to survey trade conditions and advise the Canadian people where they can do business profitably in that country.
It frequently happens in the countries where the trade commissioners are located that there may be a difference of opinion at the custom house when Canadian goods arrive there, and the trade commissioners resident in those countries and on fair terms with the Customs Department of that foreign country are able in many instances to iron out the difficulties and make it easier for Canadians to trade there. Then from time to time the trade commissioners advise the government of proposed tariff changes that might be looming up in those countries, and represent as diplomatically as possible to the people of those countries the advantages it would be to them to give fair terms to Canadian products.
Another part of the duties of the trade commissioners is this, and it is done with considerable profit to Canadian industries. A firm in Canada desiring to export products to one of the countries where we have a trade

Supply-Trade and Commerce
commissioner located, may communicate with that commissioner and ask for the names of people there who would handle Canadian products. The trade commissioner gives the names only of those whom he considers reliable. From time to time he sends reports to the office of the Minister of Trade and Commerce here, where we have in the department junior trade commissioners in training, supervisors of commercial intelligence and an editor who classifies all this information and sends it out weekly to exporters, boards of trade, banks, colleges, and generally speaking to any person who might be interested in export trade.
Since my hon. friend has invited some observations on the trade situation I would like to point out that Canada is reaching out everywhere throughout the world for export trade, and we are doing fairly well, perhaps hatter than we ourselves realize. Canada geographically speaking is as well situated as any country to do trade with the different countries of the world. If you take a look at the map you will discover the advantages we have in location, the short haul for our products to the different markets of the world as compared with other countries. Canada, as I said a moment ago, trades with the whole world, but I think we might say without disparagement to any of our smaller customers that we have nineteen or twenty first-class customers who take from us various products in agriculture, mineral, and manufactured goods. The United Kingdom is our best customer, but the United States, notwithstanding what we hear of the Fordney tariff, is a very close second. It may interest the committee to know that of our nineteen or twenty first-class customers, for the year ending 31st December the United Kingdom took from Canada $379,540,481 worth of goods; the United States took from us $349,292,392 worth -a very close second. Our next best customer was the sister Dominion of Australia with a purchasing record of $17,411,298. Japan is our fourth best customer, buying from Canada last year $15,799,800 worth. France comes next with $12,869,332; Italy, $12,195,499; Belgium, $12,014,190; and we believe that when the treaties that will be submitted to the House in a few days are proclaimed and go into effect they will add very materially to our business with France, Italy and Belgium. Our exports to The Netherlands last year amounted to $10,891,889; British West Indies, $9,306,935, plus $3,218,332 to Bermuda and British Guiana;; Newfoundland, 88.800,174; New Zealand, $7,124,598, and let me say right here that per capita we have no better
fMr. Robb.]
customer than the little sister Dominion of New Zealand, where there is an excellent feeling towards Canada. Germany, our enemy of yesterday, is to-day one of our good customers. We sold to Germany last year $7,651,117 worth of goods.
How much are we buying from Germany now?

I have not the figures just now. China including Hong Kong, which is listed separately, bought from us $5,293,808 worth; Greece, $5,964,156; Norway and Sweden, $4,597,000; Cuba, $4,905,468'; Mexico, $3,231,580. I am sure my hon. friends will appreciate that there are possibilities of greater trade development in the future with Mexico as conditions in that country become settled.
For the twelve months ending February, 1923, the total exports of Canada amounted to $92S,356,656, or an increase of 8165,808,061 over our exports for the same period the previous year. Canada is not only a large exporting nation of agricultural products, but she is becoming an exporting nation of manufactured goods. It is true that agricultural products enter largely into our exports, but it is also true that our exports of manufactured products are increasing rapidly. Canada perhaps unconsciously is becoming an exporter of manufactured goods.
I am sure it will interest the committee to have a comparison as between the exports of Canada and exports of our great neighbour to the south, the United States. For the year ending March 31st, 1922, the records of the statistical departments of the United States and of Canada show that of the total exports of these two countries, the exports of raw material of the United States were 39 per cent, and of Canada 44 per cent. Of partly manufactured products the exports of the United States were 11 per cent, and the exports of Canada 14 per cent. Of manufactured products the exports of the United States were 49 per cent, while those of Canada were 41 per cent. When we analyze our business on a per capita basis Canada ranks very high as compared with other countries. On a per capita basis the little Dominion of New Zealand comes first with an export of $154.54. Canada comes second with an export per capita of $100.63, and keep in mind that 41 per cent of that export consisted of manufactured products. The United Kingdom has an export per capita of $63.36, and the United States has an export per capita of $33.95 as against a per capita export for Canada of $100.63.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I presume I would be quite right in supposing that in manufactured exports are included such commodities as flour? That is, any goods which are not produced from the soil and sent out in the shape of raw material would be included in manufactured articles?

If we ship wheat that is a raw product. If we ship flour that is a manufactured product. If we ship milk that - is a raw product. If we ship butter that is a manufactured product. If we ship pulp-wood it is a raw product. If we ship paper it is a manufactured product. If we sfhip pulp it is partly manufactured.

The reason I asked the question is this; I take the facts to be just as the minister states them, but very often in explaining our exports I have noticed that statistics are given with the idea particularly of boosting one side or the other. So that the statistics are mixed up. For example in agricultural exports butter, condensed milk, flour, and things of that sort, are included which are really manufactured articles as my hon. friend says.

This statement has been prepared for me by the statistical department. It is without any colouring whatever and is given exactly in the form in which 9 p.m. they hand it out. Now, coming back again to the question of our exports. The total exports for the 12 months ending in February of this year were 8928,356,656, of which 42 per cent were finished products. When it is recalled that in 1890 the total exports of Canada only amounted to 8185,000,000, and that less than 6 per cent of those were manufactured products, it will be realized what great progress Canada has made in those 32 years. I would not like the House to believe that we should remain as we are with our arms folded, that we should be satisfied with our immense exports and the volume of manufactured products we are sending out. It seems to me that it should be the ambition of this country not only to increase our production but to increase the manufacture of our own products in our own country.
Hear, hear.
Converts every day.

I have in mind the days of my boyhood when many of the farms in our part of the country had a mortgage on them, and the people were struggling to build homes and become properly established with comforts for themselves and their children. They were
then breaking the land and growing a little grain, and they sometimes had to haul that grain 20, 25, 30, and even 50 and 60 miles to market. In that country to-day the conditions are changed. There are no mortgages on the farms or, if there are any, they are very few in number. The children of many of the people who then had mortgages on their farms to-day have investments in victory bonds and other securities. They possess comfortable homes, with large bams and great herds of cattle in the fields. It was the cow that paid off the mortgage on the farms in eastern Canada; and, looking at conditions throughout the country, it seems to me that we should not be discouraged for the future. The eastern provinces-the province of Ontario, the province of Quebec and the Maritime provinces-are well adapted for dairying; but there is another province in the Dominion which, perhaps, possesses as great, or even greater advantages for profitable dairying if the people there will work as the people of eastern Canada worked-I refer to the little province of Alberta. The conditions essential to successful dairying are cheap feed for the cattle, water and a good climate. I am sure no person will say that the province of Alberta has not a good climate, that it has not plenty of water, that it has not plenty of good feed for stock. I would like to remind mv fellow members in the province of Quebec_
May I interrupt the hon. minister?
Yes.
I wish to deny most emphatically that there is an abundance of feed or even of water in that province.

Well, I visited Alberta for many years annually long before my hon. friend came to this country, and if he is discouraged with Alberta, I am not. I do not believe that my hon. friend with his pessimism represents the true feeling in that province. When I remember that in the autumn of last year, at the greatest exhibition held in Canada, the province of Alberta carried off most of the best prizes for butter; when I remember that the province of Alberta is as near the sea as many ports of the province of Ontario-
Except for freight rates.
-I have no reason to feel discouraged over the future of that country. I know that dairying means hard work.

And no pay.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I am not prepared to admit that, but it means comfort, it means happy homes, it means the family united where there is work for the boys and the girls.
And fourteen hours a day.

Yes, fourteen hours a day and longer than that. But we are working fourteen hours a day in this chamber and we are doing fairly well at it. I am not making this statement with the idea of casting any reflection on my hon. friends from the western provinces, but rather to encourage them, and to say to them that what eastern Canada has accomplished, surely western Canada can do also. I am not one who believes that the son has less grip than his sire, and I believe the young men of to-day, if they are ready to get down and work as their forefathers worked, will find as good a future in Canada as in the country whence they came.

In his early remarks the minister stated that trade commissioners were in foreign countries for the purpose of advising the government. Particularly he mentioned that they were there to anticipate if any false moves, we might say, were made in connection with the tariff. Are we to understand from that that our trade commissioners are in foreign countries for the sole purpose of anticipating these tariffs, to endeavour to get as low a tariff rate for the exports of this country as possible?

I would not say that. They are there to watch conditions and to advise their government from time to time. Let me repeat again, they are there also to advise Canadian shippers of advantages in the countries in which they are located. In that connection, let me read for the information of the House a letter that I have from the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company, Regina, dated the 29th September, 1922, to our trade commisisoner in Calcutta, India:
Dear Sir,-We have to thank you tor your very comprehensive letter of August 18 giving statistics on the 1921-22 wheat crop and outlining the conditions under which India's wheat cultivation is carried on.
We note that your monthly reports are embodied m the Commercial Intelligence Journal, and as suggested by you, are taking steps to be put on the mailing list for this paper.
Then on the 11th April, they wrote for this information for a ten-year period, which Mr. Chisholm, the agent there, supplied them. Let me cite this record to show of what advantage these men are. Through the efforts of Mr. Emery, trade agent in China, of this crop there has been sold a total of 225,000 sacks of

flour shipped from the Vancouver Milling Company, the Robin Hood Mills at Calgary, the Robin Hood Mills at Moose Jaw, and the Maple Leaf Milling Company at Medicine Hat. We have also a record of a large quantity of butter which was shipped from a creamery in Alberta to China.

We are, I am sure, all very much indebted to the worthy minister for giving a few of his observations on the trade situation. I rather think he trampled on the ground of the Minister of Agriculture, and that he would have been better advised to have interested us in his travels to foreign lands. I have in mind more particularly the question which he himself raised last year, namely that our trade commissioners in some of these foreign lands were found to be doing business, as he said, due, perhaps, to the niggardliness of this particular vote or votes of a like nature, on back streets of various towns and cities. It would be very interesting to the committee if the minister would, as the Minister of Agriculture did, give us a little summary of what he found to be the condition of affairs as regards these particular officers.
A further question which I have in mind is this. Is any effort being made on the part of the Department of Trade and Commerce to secure the same trade relations between Canada and Cuba as the United States enjoy with Cuba at the present time. I hope the minister will, at least, tell us some of the things that he observed in that trip of his around the world.
I thought I had given my hon. friend a rather interesting review of trade conditions in that part of the world.
Did the minister find our trade commissioners working on back streets as he said, and does he anticipate that he will require a larger appropriation this year than in the past?

We have made a considerably increased allowance to the trade commissioners and also increased their living allowance, so that they are getting much better located than they were. In Shanghai, China, we have recently organized an exhibitios t iom, where samples of Canadian products for sale in that country are continually on exhibition. We have this on the rental basis, so that the firm shipping the goods pays a rental that almost covers the total expense. I think this is on a paying basis, or practically so.

Will the minister give me the information regarding Cuba?

Sup-ply-Trade and Commerce
As my hon friend knows, negotiations regarding tariffs are under the Department of Finance. A representative is in Cuba now watching Canadian interests.
A representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce?
Yes.
I was delighted to hear the minister speak so optimistically regarding the prairie provinces. I wonder whether his optimism is well founded.
I hope so.
I happened to be in Moose Jaw last week-
Did the hon. member meet the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) there?

This time I did not go into the barn; but I noticed in the window of one of the grocery stores, fresh eggs marked 18 cents per dozen. These came from the country; and the farmer had to pay for the crate and breakages before the eggs reached the store, and I presume there was a little profit on the crate too. I asked some of the people in the country what they were receiving for eggs and they said 14 cents. I just wonder, considering what they have to pay for their food, whether it is a profitable situation for them to sell eggs at 14 cents per dozen. I also found that dairy butter, not creamery butter, was selling at 22 cents. It does not seem to me that these prices show that the West is going to be prosperous in a very short time. It is true that we need all the markets which the minister has spoken of, and I trust by the opening up of the larger markets of the world, the price will increase and the farmer will be given a fair deal for what he is raising.
The minister has given the committee the amount of exports that Canada had during the last year. Can he give the committee the same figures as regards the imports?
I have some imports from different countries. This is not so well classified as the other. I would be glad to hand the statement over to my hon. friend if he is interested.
What is the total?
I have not the total.
The minister stated that there were practically no farm mortgages in Canada.
In the section of country where I was born and brought up.
Just that one section.

I was citing conditions in that part of the country when I was a boy when there were many mortgages. I said that to-day there were but few mortgages in that part of the country. What I said was that the people who at that time had mortgages to-day have victory bonds.

Can the minister give us some idea as to what peculiar conditions in that part of the country would be responsible for this freedom of the farms from mortgages? His statement seems an extraordinary one.
Perhaps it is the good old cow business.
A little hard work
Does the minister mean to say that we do not work hard out in the West?

I am not saying anything about the West; I am talking about the East. The hon. gentleman asked me to what cause the condition I have described is attributable. A little hard work and patience and continuous saving from year to year will bring it about.
Are there for sale any of those cows that paid off the mortgages?
Yes, not long ago, I know, one sold in British Columbia for $1,600.

A Quebec cow, sir? Is the minister aware that we have had evidence only this week from prominent men in the province of Quebec that the very conditions he speaks of actually obtain there, namely, hard work, long hours and small pay, and indeed less than small pay, rather no pay at all but a deficit instead, and that these same conditions are driving the young people off the land in that province at the present time? Is the minister aware of that?
I am told that the young people are leaving the land not only in Quebec but in old free trade England.

Well, that only proves a fact that has been well known for many years, indeed throughout the ages, that the men on the soil are expected, as they have always done and as people think they will continue to do, to work longer hours than anyone else for less money. That is the fact of the matter and we can prove it, and that is the very reason the people are leaving. The young

Supply-Trade and Commerce
people are getting educated; the boys are getting more sense. I can give you my own personal experience. I sent my boy to the Saskatoon Agricultural College and when he came back he used language which I cannot repeat in the House of Commons. It was the first time I had heard him express himself vigorously. He said, "I am not going to be such a-well, such a fool as you are." I said, "What do you mean, Jack?" He answered, "I am not going to work fifteen hours a day to grow cheap food for the man who wants to work eight." And I cannot blame him.
Are you opposed to education?
No sir, I am not; but when you educate a young man you develop his powers of comparison and when he sees one man working eight hours while he has to work fifteen, he naturally resents the idea.

Let them combine
forces and work together.
The fault does not lie with the man who has to work fifteen hours but with the man who does not want to work more than eight. Perhaps some of the evil lies in that direction.
The hon. member tells us where the cause lies, but he does not tell us who is hit in the result.
A barber works fifteen hours a day all the year round. Does the farmer in the West work fifteen hours a day throughout the whole year?
Do you think he ought to?
I am asking a plain question. Do these men in the West work on the farms fifteen hours a day all the year round?

I can answer the question so far as my own farm is concerned. We have stock on it and while the men certainly do not work fifteen hours a day throughout the entire year, in winter they work ten at the very least; and always bear in mind that they work hard on Sundays as well.

I am surprised to hear the minister make the statement we have heard this evening. I cannot speak for Quebec, of course, but the hon. member who referred to conditions there was speaking from the evidence that has been brought out in regard to that province and no doubt that is the best evidence we can have, I can, however, speak of conditions as they exist in my own province. I happen to represent as good a farming section of the country as can be found in

Ontario and perhaps as good as any in the whole Dominion, and a few weeks ago I got certain information from one of the men of the type the minister speaks of. This gentleman who is a successful farmer has been in his locality for thirty years and I want to make a reference or two to the statement he made to me. Now, the minister stated.that in eastern Ontario or Quebec, which is much the same, there are no mortgages outstanding to-day. I wish I could bring myself to think the same. As a matter of fact, and quite naturally, we have mortgages in Ontario, and I do not see any way by which we could possibly avoid having them. Let me explain why, A farmer gets a section of land, it matters not whether it is large or small. If he raises a family and puts by a little for a rainy day he is under the' necessity of mortgaging the farm, if he wants to have something to live on in his old age. Obviously therefore he cannot hand the farm over to his son without encumbrances. The son gets it with a mortgage on it and he too raises a family and naturally gets into the same position, so that again the mortgage is passed on to the next generation. If I might speak of the farm on which I live, I might remark that my son now represents the third generation holding the same homestead. For these reasons therefore it is inevitable that we shall have mortgages; and although I have not the statistics by me to give figures., I am satisfied that there are as many mortgages on our farms to-day as there were thirty years ago. I honestly believe also that the men holding these mortgages are not as well satisfied with the securities as those who held mortgages at that time.
Is there a mortgage on the holdings you have in the city of Toronto?
I do not happen to have a home in the city of Toronto.
Have you any holdings in the city of Toronto?
Yes.
For the benefit of the committee, will the hon. member give his equity in these holdings in view of the opinions he has expressed?

Wait until the time comes; I will do that later. I want to deal with the question to which the minister referred. I met at the railway station a short time ago a gentleman from the constituency adjoining my own, and I might quote what he said in a conversation we had, in order to convince the committee that some of the statements that

Supply-Trade arid Commerce
have been made in this House have not been made without some foundation of fact behind them. This man has been successful in his farming. You talk about dairy cows. For thirty years he has had as good a herd of Jersey cows as can be found anywhere in the country, and they have been as intelligently cared for. He works fourteen of fifteen hours a day, and while he was not complaining, because as I say he has been successful, he gave me some facts which I think it is well for the House to know. When I informed him of the nature of the debates that have taken place in this House he told me that he and his son had sat down and figured their profits for the year 1921, and they discovered that they had not quite a dollar a day after deducting all expenses. That is a well managed farm and I defy the minister, which is saying a good deal, to find a more successful man than this gentleman. Yet that is just what he told me a couple of weeks ago. These conditions exist whether we want to admit the fact or not; and while we are not grumbling in western Ontario, and no one can say he has heard us grumble much in this House, I do not want to sit here and have statements made which I know are not true concerning the district I represent as well as that part of the country generally. I have sat here and listened with a good deal of patience to men who have tried to be optimistic,and I can bear with them, because I would rather take an optimistic than' a pessimistic view of things generally. I do not like the world to know our actual condition. It is bad enough to let the House know, but unfortunately Hansard publishes our statements whether they are pessimistic or optimistic, and they go forth to the country. I have refrained from saying anything pessimistic, but I do not want the impression to go out to the contrary because otherwise we who know the actual conditions in our constituencies may be laughed at when we get up in this House and refer to them even in the most guarded terms. We will not stand for that. If the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) or the member for East York (Mr. Harris) wants to know particulars of what I refer to I shall be pleased to enlighten them in my room, but I am not going to publish them on the floor of the House.

I am sincerely glad to know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) and so many other hon. members are keenly interested in dairy farming. It is news to me, because I have been interested in it in a direct way all my life, but since coming to this House I have not heard very much
117	[DOT]
upon this phase of farming. I believe dairy farming in eastern Canada is perhaps the most prosperous line of agriculture which our farmers have been following, but I think the minister left an .impression which is not altogether correct. I do not know what particular part of Canada he was referring to in the very rosy picture he unfolded to us of a farming community that was encumbered with mortgages thirty or forty years ago but now enjoys prosperity in the way of comfortable homes and victory bonds. I would like to know just exactly where that favoured spot is, because from my acquaintance with the dairy industry in Ontario I very much question whether the picture truly depicts actual conditions.
I have before me evidence, some of which I laid before this House two years ago in the course of the budget debate, and which has been further confirmed since that time by Professor Leitch of the Ontario Agricultural College. Professor Leitch was brought up on a farm and educated at the agricultural college. He has had practical experience in managing farms on a commercial scale, and for a number of years past he has been making a special study of mixed farming in Ontario, both dairying and stockraising. In his sworn evidence before the Special Committee on Agricultural Conditions he gave a summary of conditions that obtained on a certain number of specially selected farms. These farms were selected as representative of average conditions in certain sections of the province, which were by no means the poorer sections. I do not wish to quote this evidence in detail, but here are some of the results which he gave to the committee and which are substantially in line with my own experience. I sincerely hope that this summary will elicit as much cheering from the members in my immediate vicinity as did the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
For the year ending May 1st, 1921, summarizing the financial operations of dairy farmers in the county of Oxford-the banner dairying county in Ontario, equal I think to the section to which the minister was referring-after allowing 5 per cent on investment and 26 cents an hour for eleven hours a day for 365 days in the year to the farmer, the cost of producing milk was found to be $2.70 per 100 pounds, while the price received was the same. The following year there was a considerable reduction in the cost of production, it dropped to $1.95 per 100 pounds, but the price received was also lower, being $1.8?



Supply-Trade arid Commerce
per 100 pounds. So that with this very moderate allowance for wages and profit the farmer was selling his milk at a loss of 12 cents per 100 pounds-that is, 12 cents per 100 pounds less "than would allow him 26 cents an hour for wages and 5 per cent on his investment. Surely no commercial undertaking could ask for a less margin of profit or a lower wage than that. Following this same calculation down for the year ending May 1st, 1923-assuming, of course, that no change will take place in the figures for the next month-on the same basis the estimated cost of producing milk will be $1.70 per 100 pounds, while the price received will be $1.65 per 100 pounds, or 5 cents less per 100 pounds than the cost of production.
Those are average conditions in the very best dairying section of Ontario. I assume that conditions are no better in the particular section to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce was referring. Although the dairy farmer is engaged in perhaps the most prosperous line of agriculture in this country, those are the results that he is obtaining at the present time, and surely the picture is not so rosy as the minister would have us believe. Those figures do not show anything unusual. There is no occasion for a dairy farmer to be alarmed at them, there is no particular reason for discouragement, because he has always had to put up with conditions such as these and very often very much worse. I do not know if they were any better at any time. Perhaps during 1918 conditions may have been just a little bit better than those figures would indicate. But those are the figures for the last three years, and they indicate in a fair way the condition of the dairy farmer to-day in this province.
Although the men of forty or fifty years ago no doubt should be accorded great credit for their energy and courage, I have it on the mthority of men who are older than the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, men who have been engaged in this work all their lives, that dairy farming at the present time is very much harder than it was fifty years ago; that farming in this part of Ontario, in the province of Quebec, entails more work, more energy, more thought, more constant application, than it did forty or fifty years ago. I believe that to be the case.
I think that is right.

If that is
the case, and if it is true, as the minister avers, that there are fewer mortgages now than there were then, I must conclude that the men engaged in this business are entitled

at least to some credit for the way they are carrying on. I question that statement, however; I doubt very much whether mortgages, even in the dairy sections of this province and the neighbouring province of Quebec, are becoming fewer. I do not wish to draw any pessimistic picture of the prospects of the dairy farmer, but I would like to have these few figures placed on record in order that an accurate estimate may be formed by hon. members who, perhaps, do not know the actual conditions of dairy farming as they exist to-day.

When the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy), who has iust spoken, said that the farmer, his wife and family work and the farmer gets the money, he stated the truth. It is true that the farmers work hard; it is true their days are long and their pay is poor. But it is also infinitely true that the farm woman's day is longer and her pay poorer. With all due deference to the superior wisdom of men, one mistake that I think the men continually make in this House is that of treating the problem of rural depopulation as a man's problem and a man's problem only. Hon. members talk about the boy getting an education, as if when you have talked about the man and the boy you have finished the family-but you have not. You want to remember that the girl is also getting an education. The girl has seen her mother work as that mother does not want her daughter to work and as the daughter herself does not want to work. If you go over a rural community to-day-take your own constituency, for example,-and tabulate the results of your observation, you [DOT]will find more young men on the land than young women: the girls leave first, and that is a pretty sure indication that the boys will leave later. I have noticed so often that the matter is looked at from the man's point of view. When a man is forced to quit farming, if you go into the case carefully you will find-and this applies to over half the cases-that he quits because of inability to carry on the work any longer. It is because the wife or the housekeeper in that house is broken down in health, or because of the woman's rebellion at the drudgery of her life. So I feel that the other view of it, the feminine view, the woman and girl part of the household, will have to be considered before the problem of rural depopulation is to be solved.
I am glad the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) is so optimistic; it is easy for people who are not farming to be optimistic. Our farm at home has no mortgage against it; there are no sons in the family

Supply-Trade and Commerce
or there would be a mortgage against it. There is some little money coming in besides that which is the direct result of farming, but we did not break even last year and will not this year. How long can anybody go on under those conditions? I sent out eight questions to 900 soldier settlers on the land in Ontario. I have received up to date possibly 400 answers. If the minister would like to have a pleasant Sunday afternoon, I will lend him these 400 answers, and if he still says there are no mortgages on the farms of Ontario I am sure that after reading the information contained in these replies he will not be so optimistic.

Being a member of this special committee which is taking evidence with regard to agricultural conditions in Canada, and being a farmer myself, I have been very much disappointed at much of the evidence we have received. 1 know that in my own province of New Brunswick the agriculturists are in very bad financial condition. We were told by our provincial government within the last six months, when we went to them for some assistance to tide the farmers over and enable them to produce a crop this year, even to enable them to stay on the land-because large numbers of them are migrating to the United States, owing to the very serious conditions prevailing here-we were told that had we been raising cattle we would to-day find ourselves in good circumstances; that had we ceased two or three years ago to grow potatoes and gone into the stock industry, we would now be in a comfortable position. I had hoped that that was the case, because if only one province of Canada was in a bad financial condition with regard to its agricultural industry, it would not be very serious.
Our committee has endeavoured to get evidence from all the provinces, and I think we have obtained evidence from most of them with regard to the agricultural conditions. I wish to state briefly some of the figures that Professor Leitch put before us-and by the way, I think his was the most convincing evidence, due to the fact that he had actual statistics. A lot of people do not take very seriously the statistics compiled at the experimental farms; they are government institutions, and whether the work is correctly done' or not it is apt to be looked upon as not carried out under normal conditions. Professor Leitch, as the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy) has said, has carried on experiments on farms under actual farming conditiorfe. He took seventeen average farms in Ontario and instituted on each an accurate system of bookmi
keeping. He visited the farms frequently through the year to see that the books were accurately kept. An account was kept of all outlay for actual operation; the farm was credited with every item of production, and at the end of the year those seventen farms had a balance on the wrong side of the ledger of. on the average $460. These seventeen farms were representative, he told us, of the best counties in Ontario; they were in one of the finest stock raising sections in the province, and on those farms dairying and the growing of fat cattle were carried on.
I thoroughly agree with the member for Glengarry when he says he believes that cattle growing and dairying are the most profitable branches of agriculture in Canada. I have come to that conclusion after listening to the evidence bf witnesses from the various provinces on the different phases of agriculture We also had before us very recently a milk dealer from Montreal who was raised on a farm, whose brothers, he told us, are farmers. He himself is not farming, but we came to the conclusion after listening to his evidence, that few of the witnesses who appeared before us understood farming conditions better. He told us of the conditions in the province of Quebec-which, by the way I looked upon as one of the most prosperous provinces of the Dominion. We had been told repeatedly that the farmers of Quebec were both prosperous and contented. I had hoped it was so; indeed, I believe it is true in larger measure of that province than it is of any other. But this milk dealer told us that due to the cost of the production of milk exceeding the price received for it, the young people were leaving the farms; they were drifting to the Canadian cities in small degree and to the United States in a much larger degree, and the consequence was that the older men were not able to carry on the operations to the extent that they formerly did. They could not afford to hire help to carry on their industry, therefore they were selling off their cattle and decreasing production; and the situation was viewed with alarm. He said the tin\e was coming in the not far distant future, when, if present conditions continued., dairying would reach the vanishing point in the province of Quebec

notwithstanding the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to-night. I cannot help thinking that the minister is living in the past; that he has not been out in the country during the last two or three years. I admit that there was a brief period during the war when farming was profitable in all its branches. I want to admit this also. I think that during

Supply-Trade artd, Commerce
the prosperous period the farmers contracted habits that would be considered more or less
extravagant by the farmers themselves, but not by city people by any means, because in the most prosperous days I do not think the farmers enjoyed anything like the luxuries and comforts that might be considered luxuries that are enjoyed by people in the cities in the very worst times. That is my candid opinion, and I have had a good opportunity for observing.
The hon. member for Calgary just now took the words out of my mouth when he asked if any of these cows were for sale that the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke of. Our committee would be glad to dispose of them at fancy prices to help pay off the mortgage on the farm and keep the farmer in comfort. We have heard from many men who have been raising cows and have been given very full statistics on production, and know something about the conditions.

I fear I have somewhat stirred up hon. gentlemen, and they are getting away from the real issue. I am bound to say I cannot quite follow all this debate. I present to my hon. friends proof taken from the statistics of the Dominion of Canada that our exports have increased from $185,000,000 thirty-two years ago to 1928,000,000 to-day. I tell them of the conditions that existed when I was a boy, when there were mortgages on the farms, and of the conditions that exist there to-day. I never pretended for one moment that farming was a very profitable proposition to-day. I know it is like most other businesses in Canada to-day, the profits are smaller than during the war period, but I maintain that there is no reason in this country for the pessimism which we have heard expressed in the House. I do not believe that sort of argument is the best thing for Canada. I was simply trying to strike a note of encouragement for my friends of the western provinces when I expressed that opinion, and it is only an opinion for what it is worth, although I am bound to say I have heard it shared in by many people. I remember not so many years ago when every Alberta man you spoke to told you that Alberta was the best province in the Dominion. Go to Alberta, was what they all said. Those were the days when the easterner was buying town lots at fancy prices. I tried to point out to my hon. friends the natural advantages of that sunny province, and I have hope yet for the province of Alberta because, geographically situated as it is, being as near to the sea as many parts of Ontario, with a fertile soil and wonderful agricultural possibilities, a
FMr. Caldwell.]
splendid supply of coal, good running water, and producing the best wheat in the world-
We can't get a price for it.
-why with such resources, should it not have a great future before it? You can use your coal and your natural gas-
Oh, oh.

-I mean the variety up ar Medicine Hat, to drive your flour mills and turn- your wheat into the best flour in the world, and have the offal to feed to dairy stock in the province. Just have a little of the courage of the early men who cleared the land in eastern Canada and things will come all right. Nobody who travels along the countryside and sees the comfortable homes and large bams and great herds of cattle in the field can fail to be impressed with these the best evidences of prosperity. Of course, there are always people who are leaving the land. I left the land myself, out of compulsion. In those days it was not so easy to get a farm as it is now. I was the elder of two boys, and I left the farm much against my will to become a miller's apprentice. My brother is on that farm to-day. He has the adjoining farms and we hope that his boys will remain there and their boys after them, because we know it is a happy and a comfortable home, and that there is a prosperity and contentment on the land that you do not get in the cities where you have to get up at the shriek of a whistle in the morning, and are fined if you are late getting to work.
That is not as bad as an alarm clock.
I agree with the hon. member across the way who said it is the woman who "works hard, and if there is any place where a woman has to work hard, it is on a dairy farm.

I have for some time been an admirer of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I am sure that he has now justified that opinion by his ability to start something. I am glad that the discussion has ,turned on subjects that are prolific of debate and with which I am intimately acquainted-dairy cows, mortgages and natural gas: I do not propose to prolong this discussion, most of which, if I may be allowed to say so, is rathej fruitless.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. member will allow me, I was just going to call the atten-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
tion of the committee to the irrelevancy of a discussion of agriculture upon this item. Unless the committee is willing to allow it, it is altogether out of order.
I think it is a profitable discussion.

I thought that possibly
owing to the absence of the Minister of Agriculture his department was being administered by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon.

He is over there
now.
He is very subdued though.

I do not wish to lead the discussion into irrelevant channels, but I do desire to say something that has not been said on this subject and which I think ought to be said, and that is with respect to the question of farm mortgages. You cannot prove anything by the existence of farm mortgages as to the prosperity or lack of it in farming, and I think I can'show why. From my knowledge of farming in Ontario there have always been farm mortgages, and I believe there always will be. Whether farming is made more profitable or not, that condition will continue for this reason: The man who is not a success on the farm, and whose farm is mortgaged, will naturally have to let it stay mortgaged because his lack of success does not enable him to pay it off. On the other hand the man who is successful, and let me say that profits on the farm are small, only succeeds in paying off his mortgage after a number of years of hard work, and by that time he is ready and properly entitled to retire. One of the boys or an immigrant buys the farm, makes a small payment and gives a mortgage to the former proprietor for the balance. So mortgages will continue. They may be changing all the time. Some men may make money, and others may lose, but owing to this continual transfer of property mortgages will continue to exist on the farms. The man who takes up farming as a means of living is a man of small means as a rule, and can only secure a farm by making a small payment and giving a mortgage for the balance. So it proves nothing as to the prosperity or lack of it in farming to point to farm mortgages, and anyone who argues from that basis is on aboslutely unsound premises. I think that is one point that has apparently been overlooked.
I would like to say further, I believe from personal experience and from some knowledge I have gained that there is a farm problem at
the present time, and if we had a little less discussion and a little more practical work I think a great deal could be done towards bringing about a solution of that problem. I propose to offer a suggestion to the House which if acted upon would do a great deal towards solving the problem. If you will bear with me just a moment or two I will attempt to do what very few have so far tried to do this session. It is a common thing to find that the man who has had no experience in a particular subject is the one who professes to know most about it. I would recommend to the government that they appoint a small committee to investigate this problem and attempt to find a solution, and I will outline what I think the work of that committee should be. First, I would ask for half a dozen members of this House who know nothing about farming by actual production but who know all about it in theory. I would also have half a dozen members of the farming group in the House-
Here is one.

-who know all about other lines of business by theory and nothing from actual practice. I would further recommend that half a dozen businesses may be acquired at the expense of the government and half a dozen farms in various parts of the country secured. Then I would reverse the existing operation and put the farmers into business and the business men on the farm where they would have the benefit of instruction from the colleges of agriculture. These men could be given a good deal of help and being intensely practical individuals -experts if I might call them such- could easily become familiar with the particular operations to which they were devoting their attention. Then, after two years had elapsed, I would let these men come together, give parliament the benefit of their experience, and recommend to this House something in the nature of a real solution for the existing difficulties. In the meantime, of course, the profits in both cases would go to the state. Now, I have something else. The undertaking in question would only employ twelve men. I would suggest that the rest of the country, while this experiment is in process, get down to hard work and stop grumbling until the committee is able to present a report.

May I ask the minister a question or two pertaining to this item. He will recall that last year when these estimates were under consideration I brought to his attention-indeed it was under his consideration as well-the question of the development of

Supply-Trade an'd Commerce
trade with certain islands in the southern Pacific, more particularly the Fiji Islands. This may, perhaps, seem to the committee comparatively insignificant, but as a matter of fact there is a prospect, I think, of developing some very excellent trade to the advantage of both parties. I received correspondence lately, and I have no doubt the minister also has, more particularly on the question of cocoanut oil, considerable quantities of which are brought into this country, and its importation. If the minister could give the committee some information in regard to that question I would like him to do so. I do not think it is necessary for me to enter into details as he knows, perhaps, the whole subject pretty fully. Before I complete this request, however, he will recall that one of the points at issue was the providing of suitable cold storage facilities on the steamers running between our Pacific coast and Australia, calling at Fiji to bring the products of Fiji to Canada. The minister will also recall this: That the market in times gone by, prior to about a year or two years ago, for Fiji fruit-pineapples, bananas and such like, was chiefly in Australia. But in that case they competed with the northern Australian product and therefore the new tariff of Australia largely shut that fruit out. On the other hand we have an excellent market for those fruits and Fiji offers a capital market for our manufactured goods. Would the minister give the committee the benefit of the latest information on these points?

I have not before me the
figures of the general trade with Fiji, but my recollection is that generally speaking the Fiji group purchases about $80,000,000 worth of goods a year, some of which products Canada might supply. Prior to the introduction of the latest Australian tariff the Fiji business was largely with the Dominion of Australia. They exported to that commonwealth considerable quantities of bananas, some oranges and pineapples; but Australia placed a very heavy duty on these imports particularly bananas. I am not just sure of the rate but it was prohibitive the hope being entertained of starting a banana industry in Australia. It was represented to the Dominion of Canada that Fiji would be a profitable source of trade for this country inasmuch as they could supply to us the bananas and other fruits which we now purchase from the Central American states, and that in return \hey would buy Canadian products.
Let me say in passing that there is some misapprehension as to the value of the Fiji market. I stopped there on the way down to
TMr. Stevens.]
Australia and met the governor and his council; in fact, travelled down with the colonial secretary, who has a summer home in British Columbia and who had gone there for a rest. They give to Canada a preference in that market. In some of the islands quite an area is devoted to raising cattle; but their principal source of revenue, as far as I could make out, would be from the production of pineapples. I am not sure that it would be possible to introduce their bananas on this market because our people have been accustomed to a banana different to the species which they produce. Also I am not very sure, from the information I gained, that the Fiji banana has the requisite keeping qualities for shipping. They had there an expert banana man who had been brought from the West India Islands, a Scotchman, and hr had hopes that they would develop in the Fijis a considerable banana business. I will ask the House to bear with me a moment while with much deference and humility I offer a few observations on the subject that is under discussion, although it is not the subject that is referred to by the motion. I was interested in the remark of the hon. leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke). He begged of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archam-bault) that as the two of them differ in their attitude towards this farmer's problem the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres would give him credit for sincerity, which he would reciprocate. I know that the request will not be denied, for the reason that it is only a few months since the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres adopted the same attitude as is now adopted by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). It is only a few months, indeed, since the difference between the sale price of the farmer and the purchase price of the consumer was laid at the door of a profiteering government by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce himself, and was laid ak the door of that awful monster, protection, by all hon. gentlemen across the
way. Consequently they should not be slow in according courteous treatment to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) while he now presses home the arguments in which they were so prolific just eighteen months ago.
Let me refer to another feature. I do not think anyone has listened to these contentions longer than I have or has been the object of them, the one to be destroyed by them, more directly than I have been. The leader of the Progressive party himself, in the fall campaign of 1921, emphasized the serious position the country was in because of the policy pursued by the then administration; because of what he alleged was the big interest affiliation of the Prime Minister of that day. Why, he said, we have the spectacle of the farmer's products going down until he cannot make a profit, while the stock of Dominion Textiles, for example, is at a figure higher by far than just a few years ago; the one is up and the other away down. The hon. gentleman had on his paint and feathers and was on the warpath to bring about a change in those conditions by political effort. Today the farmer's products are much further down, textile stock is much further up, and the leader of the Progressives has retired from politics. Why all this change? What is the cause of the intensifying, the aggravating of the condition against which there was so much thunder in the fall of 1921? There was nothing complained of in that day that to-day does not exist in intensified and aggravated form. I appeal to hon. gentlemen to my left if such is not the case. It is the case; the cost of living higher; the farmer's products selling lower all along the line; what the farmer has to buy standing up; prosperity harder to find in every part of this Dominion.
Do not be pessimistic.

No, I will not, but before I am through the hon. gentleman will understand my views on these questions; at any rate it will not be owing to lack of effort if I do not make them understood. Much of what hon. gentlemen complain of respecting the condition of farming in Canada is true. In fact, I do not know of very much they have said that is not true. The condition of farming in this country to-day is a very difficult one. The farmer is undoubtedly getting pre-war price for what he sells and is paying almost double the pre-war price for what he buys. That is true of the whole Dominion.
Is Saul also among the prophets?

"Well, Saul also may be among the prophets-I heard Saul prophesy a

year and a half ago in the person of the hon.
member for Brome, but I have not heard Saul anything like so loud in recent weeks, and I do not look for very much from him in this session. Now, in eastern Canada the pressure of these conditions does not come home in quite the same degree as it does in the West, for reasons that I will advert to later, but which for the moment I will only describe in these words: In western Canada the tendency to invest the profits of the inflation period was greater than in eastern Canada, because the land, which is the farmer's capital, was nearer at hand and more abundant. That is one reason; another is this: That the volume of purchases per man is greater in the West, and consequently when the cost of purchases rises, the western man feels it more than does the eastern farmer. Nevertheless conditions are difficult in every province. I may be asked whether I attribute this to the administration. If I followed the example of hon. gentlemen opposite I would do so. I do it in part; I believe there were variations in taxation a year ago that in at least substantial degree-material degree; put it that way-are responsible for the extra burdens the common people of this country carry now. But I do not attribute it wholly to hon. gentlemen opposite or to any policy being followed by the government of the day, it is only partly due to that, and that part, while it is material, is not the main factor by any means. Why do I say so? I ask hon. gentlemen to look the world over now, as I asked them to do two years ago and a year ago, look into other countries and ask themselves the question: Is the condition of agriculture better there than it is here? Are not the same wailings, the same cries and complaints, heard in every country of the world at this hour? Are they so loud and so fierce and so well foundationed in any country as they are in the Old Land, free trade England to-day? What is the main problem of the British government right now?
Taxation.

Taxation, yes; and they are heavily taxed. We do not know what taxes are compared to what they have over there. But agriculture over there is not specially taxed; the great burden of taxation does not fall on it at all.
What about the rents-the rent burdens of agriculture over there?

Of course they have a rent burden, but you have an interest burden in its place. The hon. gentleman attributes it to rent over there? What about Ireland? In

Ireland the rent burden has been pretty much done away with, but precisely the same conditions prevail.
Does the hon. gentleman contend that the ratio of taxation to wealth is greater in Great Britain than it is in Canada?
Yes, I think it is.
Is the right hon. gentleman certain about that?

I think it is. It is on the mass of the people. The tax in Canada on very great wealth is heavier than it is there, and the tax on the mass of the people is heavier there, although it has been made heavier in this country within the last year. Hon. gentlemen assert that there must be something wrong with government policy because agriculture is in this position and because there is a constant diminution of the proportion of agriculturists in our country to the total of population. I know it is in the minds of hon. members-I know it is not in the mind of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and never was; he only pretended it was-that this condition is due to false fiscal policy. Well, if there is a country in the world that illustrates the diminution of agricultural population more clearly and more forcibly than any other, it is Great Britain. Great Britain to-day has not more than 17 per cent of its population on the land.
Surely the right hon. leader of the opposition would never compare Great Britain with Canada on equal terms as regards agriculture?
Of course not.
Great Britain is not an agricultural country at all; it is an industrial country.

But it was pretty much an agricultural country before free trade came in; I will give the hon. gentleman the figures in a moment. I say that to-day 17 per cent
of the population of Great Britain are on the land. In the year 1850 there was over half, of the population, on the land, so that it was pretty much an agricultural country. I think that the process of diminution has been intensified there by the failure to provide a preference for the British producer in the British market. But I do not think that is the main cause in the diminution of the proportion of agriculture.

What was the population at that time? Are there hot as m*,ny on the land now as then?

Not by any means. If the hon. gentleman will read the reports of the expert committees appointed by the government of Mr. Asquith he will find that the number on the land to-day is not by thousands, nor tens or hundreds of thousands, nor by something over a million what it was then.
