Is there a country in the world to-day where there is the same percentage of agriculturists as there was fifty years ago? There is not, and I will say this further: There is no country in the world where the diminution of agriculturists in proportion to the rest of the people has been less than it has been in the Dominion of Canada.
Would Canada have had a less proportion of her people on the land today if she had not for years carried on a persistent, paid, government propaganda to put people on our vacant lands?

I think we would have had less people on the land if we had not had that propaganda, not only less on the land but less everywhere else. I do not think the propaganda has resulted in a larger or smaller proportion on the land. I think it has resulted in a somewhat larger population, more on the land and more elsewhere as well. I do not think it has affected the proportion by any perceptible amount whatever.
I was speaking of the Old Country. Now I come back to Canada. I ask hon. gentlemen to inquire and tell me of a country in the world where the proportion of agriculturists to-day as compared with fifty or eighty years ago is as great as it is in Canada. I do not think there is one. I know the United States is not one. I know Great Britain is not one. Great Britain has gone down from nearly sixty per cent to about seventeen per cent, where it is to-day.
Was there any other country that had the same amount of free land to exploit?

The United States had. Australia had, the Argentine had-all these
new countries of the world had. I do not know that they had as much fine new land for agricultural purposes as we had, and if we had the more that would be one reason why we have diminished less than they have, and what the hon. gentleman has in mind would be right. But what is the fundamental cause of the diminution of the proportion of agriculturists in the Dominion, in the United States, in Great Britain, in France, in Germany, in Australia, in every country in the world? Surely it is not because the people the world over have been following mirages in fiscal policies, have not had brains enough to see what is the right and proper course. We cannot come to that conclusion, because while one country has followed one course, another has followed another, and it so turns out that those who pursued the policy of free trade have found their proportion of agriculturists come down most rapidly of all.
Does the hon. member mean to say that there are vacant farms in Great Britain?

I have seen them, but I would not say there are vacant farms where the land is good and reasonably fit for agriculture. I do not know whether there are pr not, I know that land has gone out of cultivation and into grazing to the extent of millions of acres. However, that is not the point. I am trying to deal with the matter in the large. There are influences of a minor character that are different in one country from another, but when you find every country has its urban population multiplied and its rural population diminished, you must look for something more basic than anything that is peculiar to the individual country.	_
What is it that is basic? Why surely it is this, and this is not anything new on my part. I was seeking to make this clear to the Prime Minister when 1m was leader of the Opposition, and I did not have much success. 1 will have far better success to-night. I know it was understood then thoroughlv by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The fact is we do not require as large a proportion in the world to-day to produce what the farmer produces for the world as we did in those times. Why do we not? Some would say, because we have machinery which produces more rapidly, we do not need as many on the land. That is true, but that is not the main cause in my opinion, for the reason that we have also machinery in other occupations of life producing other goods much more rapidly than they were produced in olden times. It is

Supply-Trade and Commerce
one of the reasons, however, because the multiplication of production by machinery is more emphatic on the land than it is in many others of the occupations of mankind.
But the main reason to my mind is this, that with the advance and evolution of civilization the needs of the human race multiply, the demands of the human race multiply. They multiply in one field after another, in the field of what we wear, in the field of the amusements necessary to entertain us, in the field of travel. In all the different spheres of this life the demands of the world are getting greater, more complicated, more multiplied, and it takes a bigger proportion to cater to these demands to-day than it did in days gone by. Where an hon. gentleman to-day travels at the rate of a thousand miles a year his grandfather travelled at the rate of a hundred miles a year. It takes men to conduct that travel. It takes a part of the world's population to provide the facilities and see that these things can be done. Then there are a thousand engaged in amusing the world to-day where only fifty were engaged seventy-five years ago. That is all consuming a portion of the population, and consequently, because of that continuous process that has been going on for decades, the world does not need and therefore the world does not employ as many in producing the single article of food of which the human being consumes just as much to-day as it did half a century ago, just as much and no more. I have tried to make clear what I regard as the fundamental cause, and what I think economists-I do not pretend to be one myself-regard as the fundamental cause of a process that is world wide.
The hon. member, I think, has given us a complete outline, but he has missed the point.
What is the point?

The point is this. The wealth has to be produced from thfe land just as much as it ever had to be, and those on the land to-day have to cater to a much larger population than formerly. That is one of the reasons why agriculture to-day is in such poor shape. We have radio and other inventions that must be paid for. How are they paid for in Manitoba, let us say? Largely from the products of the soil. Consequently the soil is more and more taxed to pay for all these luxuries.
I do not think the hon. member's mind is on the right line. If, of course, we assume that the farm pays for everything-	.
I do not say that exactly.
That is the line of MS' reasoning.
There is no wealth in Canada but what is produced from the natural resources of the country.
Or in any other country.
Well then, the more luxuries are multiplied, the heavier the burden becomes on those who produce the primary wealth of the country.

I do not see that at all. Any man who works, whether he works at the basis or at the top, whether he is working to bring the gold out of the mine or the coal, or working to turning those products into something else, every man is contributing to the world's wealth.
Excuse me again. Does the hon. member think that the man who is working at the production of radio apparatus is as necessary to the human race as the man who is producing a bushel of wheat?
Not at all.
Then why put them on a level?

I was not putting them on a level. I say that every man who produces of the world's wealth, whether he is producing at the top, at the acme of the last effort of manufacture, or at the very bottom out of the soil is contributing to the world's wealth.
I do not deny that.

That is all I stated, but the idea, to my mind, is entirely erroneous that the more the world enjoys the more those on the soil have to pay for it, work and bear. It is not so at all. No man is compelled to stay on the soil in any free country. There are those who think a terrible calamity has occurred if their son leaves the farm and goes to the city. I have no sympathy with that view whatever. I think the future of our land depends upon the growth of boys on the farm and their maturing not only into farm life but into all walks of life. The greatness of our nation depends upon the young farmer who is getting into other walks of life as well as producing sufficient of the products of the farm to meet the economic needs of the country in which he is bom. When a man finds he can do better elsewhere, his country has no call on him to stay on his father's farm. If he thinks he can do better any where else he has

Supply-Trade artd Commerce
just as good a right as any other man to get into another field. It is a free country and he can go where he thinks he may do better. We are producing proportionately far more than we did years ago. We are producing far more grain. If we produced twice as much I do not think it would be any better for those who were producing it-it would be worse. Let those who wish go where they can be best employed to their own advantage and in my judgment in so going and so acting they are doing the best thing for the country in which they live. There will still be plenty of wheat produced, there will still be plenty of barley produced, and it may be that prices will be higher because there will not be so many working at it. Then we will get that readjustment for which we are waiting.
We are however suffering much to-day from a condition which I think is more or less artificial. Time will have to cure it, and such measures as will tend to cure it should be adopted. In the world to-day, by virtue of the power of organization, those engaged in other walks of life have an advantage over those employed upon the land. Because of the power of labour to organize owing to the uniformity of the work in which they are employed, they have been able to hold up the production costs of goods made elsewhere than upon the land. Had the farmer equal power of organization-he has an equal right-then he would be in a position to obtain results parallel with the results of those engaged in production in other fields.
My right hon. friend has got my point of view exactly; he has stated everything I have been trying to get at.

I am very glad if that is so, but I was dealing with another phase of the subject. I am trying to show now the cause of the extreme feature of present conditions.
It is not due to the fiscal policy 11 p.m. of one country as opposed to the fiscal policy of another. It is due to something far more basic, namely, what I mentioned first. But this affects the situation too: There is an artificial element in production of another character. Much can be gained by the economic organization of the agriculturists of the country. The economic organization of agriculturists is an essential thing and must be perfected in this country far further than it is especially in organization for distribution. Organization will come that will control the total output of the farmer's products and thereby make his sale price bear some relation to his cost of production just as is enabled to be done in other fields of production. How long that will be in coming no one can foresee; but there will be far more effective organization, economic organization, of the agriculturists of this country; and I hope I will not be accused of political prejudice-much less any other kind of prejudice- if I suggest that if the efforts of the agriculturists of Canada had been directed on economic lines for concerted production

 or indeed, restriction of production-in fields that were shown not to be successful; more economic distribution' of the products of the farm, more direct distribution of those products to the consumer than we have through the cumbersome system of	to-day-if
that, had been the main object of agricultural organization in Canada, instead of the attainment of political power, it would have been better for the farmers of this country. I hope I shall not be misunderstood as attempting to say that I have any objection, or that anybody has any objection, to the farmers obtaining political power. Not at all, they have the same rights as any other people in this Dom-inibn; but there cannot be anything gained by a political farmers' party.
There can be a lot gained by economic organization amongst farmers. Where it ha3 been directed along that line great results have been achieved. They have been achieved more easily, I think, in smaller and more compact countries of less diversified conditions. There conditions more readily lend themselves to organization. Great things have been done in Belgium, in Holland, and in other countries of that character. They have also been done in larger countries. Even in the United States the farmers have achieved great results, when they have centred their energies upon economic organization and have not launched into other fields.
Now, having advanced these ideas I want to emphasize again that I do so certainly out of no prejudice to any part of our population. I do not pretend to have any special knowledge of farming; I have never sought to impose a knowledge of farming either on this House or any audience; but I think I know something of farm conditions. Before I take my seat, let me say that I do not pay very much attention to the evidence of any man no matter how expert as to whether farming pays or whether it does not pay. You can bring an expert to try and show what a thing costs and what it sells for by taking so much an hour for 11 hours a day in the case of a farm; and you can get a result that will show that no class of farming pays in any part of the country. But I have been on land

Supply-Trade artd Commerce
when we had to sell farm products

dairy products-at less than the worst quotations-yes, less than one half the worst quotation-offered by any hon. member in this House, and I know that on that farm the mortgage was paid off, I know that a large family was given an education. I venture to say that if Expert Leitch had got into the recesses of the house on that farm and had got at the same material that he got at to come before this committee, he could have shown there was a loss on the operations of that farm every year. I do not know how we are going to get reliable or useful statistics as to what a bushel of wheat, or a quart of milk, or a pound of butter costs. With all deference I venture to say it cannot be done but I do know of farmers who through good and bad times, through difficult weather as well as through fair weather, have managed to make comfortable homes and comfortable fortunes, have managed to raise creditable and useful families, and such is the best proof that agriculture has paid in general. In the stage at which we are now I know there will be little money made, I know that manjr will go back, but these things adjust themselves as time moves on. What we are suffering every country in the world has gone through; and the way we can accelerate the return of better times is firstly by better organization; secondly, by intelligent direction; and, thirdly, lightening the taxation burden by economies in overhead expenditures which, in the case of a country, means economical administration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Mr. Marcil, Bonaventure): It is my duty to warn the committee once more, as I have done already, that we have wandered far away from the item under consideration and unless it is the wish of the committee to proceed I must call hon. members back to a consideration of the question. I will read the resolution, if necessary, unless the committee wants to suspend all rules and continue discussing the condition of agriculture.

I did not intend to take part in this discussion but there have been some observations made by the right hon. leader of the Opposition which impel me to say a few words. The speaker in one breath advised the farmers of this country to be more businesslike, and to get organized better both for production and for marketing. I would ask the House to consider whether there can be any organization of production if you are to remain in happy ignorance of the cost of production, and I would make the

point, that the experts who have come before the committee which has been examining into agricultural conditions have endeavoured to apply business principles to farming and to the question of whether or not it ever has been possible, is possible, or will be possible in this country to make farming pay on a purely commercial basis. It is well that the real facts should be known and that the' people should find out where they stand. I always like to listen to the leader of the Opposition, and I felt a thrill of pride pass through me to-night when from his remarks I gathered that he had not been hearing my voice as often as he was accustomed to, and that he did not expect to hear it for some time to come on such a subject as this. That is one of the reasons why I hasten to correct that impression.
I want first of all to direct the attention of the committee to what I would call an historical inaccuracy in the argument of the leader of the Opposition. He will persist in his contention that free trade hurt agriculture in Great Britain. May I tell him and this committee that the agriculturist of Great Britain, that is the man who was actually doing the work on the land, the working agriculturist who had been an independent person for some generations before, by 1835 to 1840 was almost a serf working for another man, or as one of them said, "I be protected and I be starving." I do not forget that when I was a boy in Scotland, an old lady, who remembered those days, told me that before the abolition of the Com Laws in Scotland, the people went hungry. That was the condition in which agriculture was before the elimination of the Corn Laws. It was such a condition that not only the intellectual people, but the sympathetic and kind-hearted people of England, rose in their might and did away with that economic injustice which then existed.
The right hon. gentleman went on to say-

Before the hon. gentleman proceeds, does he dispute the fact that practically the entire body of agriculturists of England resisted the abolition of the Corn Laws, just as practically the entire body is asking for protection on their products to-day.

The right hon. member is wrong in his history. I have given a certain amount of sympathetic study to the history of England between 1815 and 1846. During the Napoleonic wars the landlords of England made a great deal of money. The farmers of England occasionally made money, but in times of scarcity they made tremendous profits out of their poor fellow citizens. Then the landlords raised the rents and there was not

' Supply-Trade and Commerce
any great profit for the farmers. The landlords got a great deal of money during the Napoleonic wars. After the Napoleonic wars were over after 1815, the cost of wheat, of com, of other cereals, dropped in the old country; but rents did not drop. What happened was this, that the landlords of England, who controlled both houses of parliament, the House of Lords and the House of Commons in England, imposed by law, semi-starvation on the vast body of the English people, the poor folk. They prohibited the entrance of corn into England until corn was 80 shillings a quarter. That was the law of 1815. In 1827, they inaugurated a sliding scale which very little helped the situation. The British workmen always protested against that. Finally, after years of agitation, a few British manufacturers formed the Anti-Com Law League in 1837 or 1838. After eight years of one of the most wonderful popular agitations that ever took place in any country, they converted the people to their views. First of all they had to convert the workmen in the towns. The workmen in the towns were not sympathetic to the Anti-Com Law League at first. They thought it was a " bourgeois movement," to use the expression of to-day. They thought it was a "masters' movement." John Bright and Richard Cobden converted the workmen in the towns. Then they went out and they were able to convert the agricultural labourers. As time went on they were able to convert the farmers, and finally they were even able to convert a certain number of landlords, and certain great lords and territorial magnates rallied to their cause. A Tory premier, Peel, who had been elected in 1841 as a protectionist, against the Whigs, who at that time were more or less free-traders, saw that if Great Britain was going to be saved from the social disturbances which took place and which caused tremendous revolutions in 1848, if they were to preserve the British constitution, there was nothing to do but to do away with this economic injustice and to wipe out the Corn Laws. That is a plain, unvarnished and inadequate statement of what happened in connection with the elimination of the Com Laws in Great Britain.

History repeats itself.
Mr. McMASTER; History repeats itself but in a different fashion,. The people who were suffering through economic injustice in England, were those who suffered from the power of certain people, who had a home market for all that they could produce, maintaining prices at an arbitrary level through
legislation. To-day the revolt against protection, against a high tariff in this country, comes from people who are able to produce far mote than they consume and who wish to compete in the markets of the world on a fair basis with their competitors from other lands, just as the British manufacturer or the British workman who at that time could manufacture far more than Was required to supply the people of Great Britain, wished to send on equal terms his goods to South America, Europe and elsewhere in the world Great Britain adopted a policy of free trade. Capital and labour were then free to seek the greatest economic returns. There has been a certain diminution of the rural parts of England; but the rural labourer of to-day is in an infinitely better position than his grandfather was when he and the farmer who farmed the land and the landlord who owned the land were protected by a high tariff on what they produced. Jf men came into the towns of Great Britain from the country places, that was not only because they wished to earn better wages, but because there was in many an English village-this did not apply to Scotland to such an extent-a petty tyranny of vicar and landlord, which the spirits that desired freedom could not endure. It was only in the eighties that the farmer had the right to shoot hares that were destroying his growing crop. If he did that before then he might find himself in difficulty before the bench of magistrates.
What is the fundamental cause of hard times among the farmers? The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) showed himself, as all men of sense should be, sympathetic with the conditions of the farmer. But he seemed to think that this was a worldwide condition. It is not, altogether. If you look at Europe you will find that the peasant is about the only man there who is really getting on at all well. In Europe a vast number of people have been reduced from the level of being able to eat bread to what in the old days of protection in Great Britain used to be known as the potato level, when people had to eat potatoes and rye because they could not afford wheat and wheaten bread. The fundamental ' difficulty of the situation to-day is that the purchasing power of Europe has depreciated because of the war and the inability so far of the European peoples to settle their disputes on a reasonable basis, in view of the fact that each one, afflicted with an extravagant development of the protectionist virus, has raised tariffs against the other and made the position much worse than it would have been had they only allowed trade to flow between the different
REVrSED EDITION

Supply-Trade and Commerce
countries on that continent. It was a fine thing in one way to allow the national aspirations of the different races in Europe to find expression in the formation of free states. But when these states have raised tariff barriers against the other they hurt themselves to an enormous extent.
I have just one more word to say. There is something in what the leader of the Opposition says, that there are a relatively smaller number of people required to grow food than was the case years ago, and that occupation for the surplus-those who are released from the land-is found in the fact that although people can eat only three meals a day-I think if they live in England they can eat five, although in this country they eat three a day-they can wear any amount of clothes and use any quantity almost of the necessities and luxuries of life all of which things must be manufactured. There is something in that. That may have something to do with the relative diminution in the rural population of any country. But I respectfully submit to the committee that Canada is about the last country in the world where that principle should have had application, because I know of no country, except perhaps the Argentine republic or Australia-and Australia only to a certain extent, for the whole northern half of that country is so warm that it is difficult for white men to live there- I say I know of no other country in the world where that principle should have been applied. It seems to me that it should have come into Canada later than it would anywhere else, and I am afraid that we have suffered concurrently with the rest. But what I would point out is that Canada has not only in the past forty years suffered a diminution in her rural population; we have failed to keep our immigration as well as our natural increase either in the cities or in the country. That is the serious question before the people to-day, The farm is the reservoir of man-power, says the leader of the Opposition. I agree with him. He and many other men in this country and in this House are striking examples of the contribution which the farm has ma'de to the city. But it is a mistake to drain the reservoir too much; it is a mistake to kill the goose that lays the golden egg.

I do not like to interrupt the debate, but I would observe that there has been no criticism whatever of the item under consideration. It represents a reduction of $10,000 while we show an increase of business of $165,000,000. At tljis late hour I think we might adjourn the debate upon the fiscal

policy of the country until the budget comes down.

But it shows something more than that. The cost was the same when we had a business of several millions more than now, so that the argument of the minister would not be of much value. Possibly I might be allowed to move the adjournment of the debate after I have offered some remarks. I did not think I had ventured to discuss the fiscal issue as such; that was not my object. The part of my remarks to which the hon. gentleman took exception was my statement that the state of prosperity of the British farmer would, I thought, be better today had he had a fair preference in the market he himself contributed to build.
That is, the home market? .

Yes; the hon. member
takes exception to that statement. He states that though the agriculturist was the last to be converted, he really was converted to free trade before it carried. Well, his statement is that of a man living seventy years after. I will refer him to a speech of a public man at the time that this contest was on, just about the period when the Com Laws were abolished; and I'will tell him where he can find that speech. This man was himself a free trader, and I rather think, had I been in his position at that time, I would have been one too. But I would not have been one had I been a British agriculturist.
You would have been had you been a farm labourer.

I do not know how the
farm labourer would get on unless the farmer prospered.
The landlord took it mostly in the rent.
I do not think there was any great difference of view between the farmer and the farm labourer.
Oh yes, there was.

If the hon. gentleman will read the speech of Thomas Babington Macaulay, after his election in Edinburgh, when he returned to his constituency to thank the electors, he will find one very significant commentary on the election which that gentleman had just been through, that being about the year 1849. Macaulay said: In my county I had the greatest difficulty in ascertaining where my opponents stood on the issue of free trade. When I got to the city I found

Supply-Trade and Commerce
large posters, "Vote for Smith and Free Trade," and as soon as I got into the rural districts I found equally large placards, "Vote for Smith and Protection."
But Disraeli said, within two or three years of that, that protection was not only dead but damned.

Yes, because the population of the cities was increasing rapidly, and was greater than the population of the country; and of course there were some in the country who were in favour of the other policy. But I was not arguing the general issue; I have done that before and I will do it again at the proper time. I only rose to furnish some evidence of what actually was the division of opinion in England at that time. I have done so, and the hon. gentleman can find the reference I have given him within a few yards of where I sit. As to the condition of opinion now on this question, I do not know that I can do anything better than point to the report of the committee established to look into the condition of British agriculture and to devise some means of extricating it from the calamitous situation in which it finds itself to-day. That report recommends one principle and one principle only, that of protection; and the committee heard British agriculturists fully before submitting its report. It may be that the peasant of Europe is in a rather better situation than the other stricken elements of that disaster-pursued continent. That may be true. But I wonder if that is true in Great Britain. Europe is not a free trade body of nations; it is a protected group of countries. It is only in Great Britain where we find a government appointing commissions to discover some cure for the distracted state of the agricultural population. And the cure they recommend is the one I have just outlined to my hon. friend.
Now, I always admire fidelity, even though it is blind fidelity, and I have no objection at all, in fact I hope the hon. member believing as he does-and I have not the least doubt of his sincerity-will continue to air his opinions in this House and to press them home. But I sympathize with him now in that whereas in the last parliament he enunciated and propounded those views to the applause of two parties, he has now to be content with the applause of only one.

I think it is about time to call the attention of the committee once more to the circumstances that I allowed the departure from the rule in the first instance because I was told there was *no objection to the discussion; but it is altogether irrelevant and out of order.
I shall be very brief, Mr. Chairman.
I must apply the rule.

I was stimulated to rise by the remarks of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). I think his attitude of mind is to be commended, although the process of his reasoning is open to criticism. I think the spirit he has shown is what we want to see manifested to a greater extent in this House, where there should be a serious effort to settle the problem that confronts our agriculturists. However, we have had the experience of seeing the subject treated more or less lightly, and consequently the note of seriousness voiced by the leader of the Opposition is very welcome to my ears. I am one of those who admires the rare quality of the right hon. gentleman's mind, but listening to him to-night I regretted that it was not engaged in a better cause. Circumstances have placed him in a position where he has to main-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
tain a dead issue; but I think if Providence had dealt with him differently we would have found him addressing his mind, as he did tonight, effectively to living problems, much to our satisfaction.
Now, he referred to the comparative conditions prevailing throughout the countries of the world with regard to agriculture, and he specified Great Britain in particular. I do not think that agricultural conditions in that country are commensurable with agricultural conditions in Canada. Farming is altogether a different proposition in the two countries. But there is,one relevant point; the farmer in Great Britain believes he is the victim of fiscal conditions; the farmer in Canada believes the same. It makes no difference that in Great Britain the complaint is based upon the operation of free trade, while in Canada it is based upon the operation of protection, the principle is the same. Agriculture whether in Canada or Great Britain is suffering from the social policy of the respective countries. The social policy in Great Britain is free trade, and with all due deference to the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) I must say that the British farmer has suffered from that policy.

If the British farmer
suffered from the introduction of free trade, how was it that rents went up from 1846 until about 1870, when vast quantities of cheap cereals coming from the newly opened lands of the western part of the United States brought rents down?

I think the hon. gentleman
will admit that rents in Great Britain are not closely related to the prosperity of the farmer.

The British farmers
have to make a certain amount of money before they can pay rent to their landlords.

I think the hon. gentleman
must admit that the present attitude of the British farmer is sufficient evidence that he believes the fiscal policy of Great Britain is detrimental'to his interest.

Some British farmers
want to keep our cattle out, others want to let them in so they can finish them. There is a difference of opinion.

I do 'not want to delve into
history, but I know that the British farmer since the abolition of protection has been a consistent supporter of the protectionist party. No matter where his labourer stood, the British farmer has always stood for protection. But that is not the point. I am trying to show that in Great Britain the farmer has
'Mr. Bird.l
been the victim of a social policy, and I contend that he was rightly asked to suffer because he was in the minority. The social prosperity of Great Britain depended at the time upon the acceptance of free trade; the social prosperity of Great Britain to-day depends upon the maintenance of free trade, and the British government has had to turn down the request of the farmers for protection on that very account. The present British government is a Conservative government, predisposed to protection, and yet it has- said to the farmer:	We cannot grant you protection
because it would be against the social interests of this country. So the British farmer at the present time, no matter what he has been asked to do in the past, has for the moment been called upon to sacrifice himself for the social prosperity of his country.
Has not that been the case in Canada? Has not the farmer here in the last generation or two .sacrificed himself for the social prosperity of the country? From the beginning this has been a social policy. The agriculturists of Canada have been asked and are being asked to sacrifice themselves for the social prosperity of the nation. I contend that whether in Great Britain or here what is wrong socially cannot be economically sound. That is the position the British government is taking now, and I suppose that the protectionist in this country takes the same attitude.
We ask ourselves, in the condition we are now in, in a preponderatingly agricultural * country; can we afford to take that attitude ? Can we afford in the interests of Canada as a whole to ask agriculture to sacrifice itself? When the farmers of England approached their government they said: Now, farming is either an economic or a social proposition. You have .either got to let it rest on an economic basis and accept the results, or you have to treat it socially; and if you treat it socially you have to grant it either protection or a subsidy. Those are the two propositions that the British farmers put before their government. But the present British government, which is a protectionist government, said: "We cannot give you either a subsidy or protection, because we believe it would be against the best interests of the country to do so." In Canada we have to face the question of the social welfare of all the people. If it is the desire or if it is thought right that Canada should sacrifice the farmer for the rest of the people, well, we have nothing to say. The farmers in England have nothing to say. They have accepted the decision of the government and they have to govern themselves accordingly-to go out of

Supply-Trade and Commerce
business, if necessary, in order to save the country socially. Are you going to sacrifice the farmer of Canada economically in order that Canada socially may prosper? That is the position you are up against. You cannot laugh this thing out of court; it will come up recurrently and will have to be faced.
I shall not go into the argument of the right hon. leader of the Opposition in regard to the diminution of the proportion of the population engaged in farming. I think that in that respect he got beyond his depth. It was all very well for him to argue that agriculture had diminished relatively with respect to numbers, with respect to its size. That is to say, the more shoes you put on the people's feet the less food you have to put into their stomachs, or the more you amuse their minds the less you will have to satisfy their appetites, and so on. You can argue along these lines, but you do not touch the point we are dealing with to-night. It may be true that agriculture is diminishing proportionately, but why should that be the basis of a contention that agriculture should at the same time diminish relatively with respect to its economic standing. Why should the farmers be worse off than they are to-day, even though they are less in number? According to the usual methods of reasoning, if the farmer belongs to a more exclusive set and ministers to a larger body of people, he ought to be better off than he was before; but that is a point that the right hon. gentleman altogether shelved.
Let me say a word in conclusion in respect to the right hon. gentleman's remarks concerning organization. We all know on this side that organization is of great value to the farmer, as it is to any other class in the community. The right hon. gentleman is not here but I would like to ask him what his definition of economics is, and what his definition of politics is-where he draws the line between the two. He received a great deal of applause from his own followers when he deprecated the entry of the farmers of Canada into politics, and yet he wanted the farmers to organize in their own interests. Where, in his opinion, do economics end and politics begin? What is the theory of government and the functions of government? What does he expect the government to do for the people or for any class of the people? What is the duty of the government toward the farmers or the manufacturers or other classes of the community? Is it simply to prevent individuals in each class from picking the pockets of individuals in the other classes, or see that the individuals in one class do not brutally knock down members of the other
class? I do not think so. The duty of this government is to adjust the relationship that exists between the different classes of this country, to see that one class is not unduly profiting at the expense of another.
The Farmers' party is here to-day because it has come to the point where it fails to see any dividing line between politics and economics. We are here as an economic group and not as a political group. We do not want political power; the aspirants to political power are opposite and to our right, not here. We are here as the exponents of certain economic principles, and that is what we stand for. We are not here in any narrow group sense; we are here with varied interests, but those interests all converge on the one principle of a proper adjustment' as between the different classes that make up this Canada of ours. I would like to meet the right hon. gentleman on his own ground and ask him whether the manufacturers have not profited by going into politics. Why, have other classes entered politics? Because they do not see any difference between their economic and their political interests. I suggest that there be a little more consistentcy in the definition of terms. We are living in the past when we think of politics as some sacred arena into which the ordinary people may not enter unless they take off their shoes at the gate. That belongs to the past-that policeman theory of government, that idea that the government has nothing to do with the real problems of the people.
It ill becomes the leader of the Conservative party to try to keep economics out of politics, because if any party were responsible for desecrating the sacred realm of politics by the introduction of economics, it was the Conservative party. When the Liberal government in England of the last century stood with arms upraised in horror at the invasion of economics into English public life it was the Conservative party that ruthlessly tried to bring it in, that tried to get rid of that theory of laissez faire and of the devil take the hindmost. The Conservative party in England tried to do that, while the Liberals were endeavouring to apply the policeman theory of government. We are not politicians in this group; you have noticed that many times. But we do pretend in a small way to be economists in a practical sense; that is, we know where the shoe pinches. You remember Kipling's story of the butterfly and the poor toad under the harrow. We have instances in this House of the butterfly giving good advice to the poor toad that feels every spike in the harrow. We do not pretend to be introducing radical notions into this House but we do

pretend to be bringing the actual conditions to the notice of hon. members and of the government. You experienced politicians, you statesmen, you people who have been walled up here for years living in a false atmosphere *-we are trying to let daylight into you. We are accused of preaching blue ruin in this quarter of the House. Why, in the last century every man who tried to get a square deal for the public was called a blue ruin preacher. Some hon. members say they think it is a pity that we should preach blue ruin: I say it is a pity we should have to preach it. I was back home for a few days last week, and I called my executive together. A man of long experience stood up and said: "I can tell you from my experience that more than fifty per cent of my neighbours are hopelessly insolvent, and mind you, I come from a place that is called one of the gardens of the West, where farmers might be expected to prosper." The galleries of this House have ears, the reporters' gallery, has ears, and I hope that the benches on the floor have ears, but there should be a difference in the way our plea is heard when we come with our tale of woe. It should not be received critically on the floor of the House here. It should be received rather sympathetically and with some insight into the motive with which it is given, because we do not speak these things to the public. We forget the galleries when we speak; we do not know they are there. We do not know the reporters' gallery is there. We are speaking to you, and we do not expect you to blurt these things out all over the world. We are reasoning with you because you are the people with power in your hands to remedy these things. Who else can we go to for remedy? You cannot expect us to let these things ferment in our minds in silence. This is the place where complaints should be made, and this is the place where complaints should be heard, and heard sympathetically, with a statesmanlike breadth of mind and spirit.
I am sorry to have detained the House. I know a lot of this might have been said at another time, but it will not now be said at another time, so there is no time lost.
